text: Adopt an ADR fixing the license for all new native kernel code, with options GPLv2-only, GPLv2-or-later, and dual GPLv2/MIT for reusable abstractions.
rationale: Code linked into a GPLv2 kernel must be GPLv2-compatible, and the choice decides whether kernel-side abstractions can ever be shared with permissive userspace.

text: Publish a kernel dependency license allowlist that forbids Apache-2.0-only, CDDL and other GPLv2-incompatible code, requires vendored Rust crates to be taken under their MIT option, and enforce it in CI.
rationale: The Rust ecosystem defaults to MIT OR Apache-2.0 and Apache-2.0 alone is GPLv2-incompatible, so one unchecked crate can make the kernel undistributable.

text: Decide and document whether the native kernel ABI headers and syscall surface carry a Linux-syscall-note-style exception so native userspace programs are never derivative works of the kernel.
rationale: Permissive SDK licensing and proprietary native applications rest on ambiguity unless the exception is explicit for the new ABI.

text: Define a written license firewall that maps each stability layer to a license class: Layer 1 kernel GPLv2, Layers 2-4 permissive.
rationale: It mirrors the architectural firewall and prevents copyleft from leaking upward into platform interfaces and the SDK.

text: Decide the license for native userspace platform services (compositor, package manager, personality glue, system services) among MIT, Apache-2.0, MPL-2.0 and dual MIT/Apache-2.0, including whether an explicit patent grant is required.
rationale: Every service written from V0.5 onward needs a header on day one and retroactive relicensing needs every contributor's consent.

text: Decide the license of the native SDK, runtime and language bindings and state explicitly that proprietary native applications are permitted.
rationale: Gaming and commercial software are product objectives, and developers will not target a platform whose SDK terms are unclear.

text: Decide that IDL compiler output is owned by the compiler's user with no copyleft obligation and encode this generated-code exception in every emitted file header.
rationale: Generated stubs land in every application, so unclear terms would contaminate the whole ecosystem.

text: License core platform interface definitions (IDL files and the ABI specification) under a permissive specification license with a royalty-free patent non-assert so third parties may reimplement them.
rationale: A decades-long ABI must be reimplementable by other kernels and runtimes without legal exposure.

text: Require SPDX-License-Identifier headers on every source file and gate merges on a license-header linter.
rationale: Per-file license clarity is the basis for every later scan, SBOM and compliance claim.

text: Produce a machine-readable SBOM (SPDX or CycloneDX) for the kernel, every package and every system generation, keyed by content hash.
rationale: GPL corresponding-source obligations and the EU Cyber Resilience Act both require knowing exactly what shipped.

text: Build a license-scanning pipeline over all vendored and dependency sources with a zero-unknown-license CI gate.
rationale: Manual review does not scale to a kernel fork plus a package ecosystem.

text: Publish a userspace dependency license allowlist that excludes AGPL, SSPL, BUSL and similar source-available licenses from the default image and SDK dependency tree.
rationale: Network-copyleft and non-open licenses would impose obligations on users and application developers that the platform cannot honor.

text: Provide corresponding source for every distributed binary generation: exact commits, patches, build scripts and toolchain, published alongside the binary channel and reachable from os history.
rationale: GPLv2 section 3 obligations begin with the first public binary release and generations make the mapping precise.

text: Ship a third-party notices bundle and an About/licenses view in the installer and Settings that exposes all license texts and the GPL written offer.
rationale: Notice preservation is a hard requirement of nearly every license in the image.

text: Audit every linux-firmware blob and vendor firmware used on target hardware for redistribution terms and define a firmware policy of ship, download-on-demand, or exclude per blob.
rationale: Several firmware files are non-redistributable and shipping them in an image is infringement.

text: Adopt an ADR on proprietary GPU kernel drivers (NVIDIA proprietary module versus open kernel modules, Nouveau and NVK) covering GPL-only symbol exposure, tainting and support commitments.
rationale: GPU support is the hardest hardware blocker and the licensing posture determines which path is even possible.

text: Define the out-of-tree and proprietary kernel module policy for the fork: whether native kernel objects are exported GPL-only, module signing enforcement and taint semantics.
rationale: Vendors and users will ask whether they can load third-party modules and the answer must be settled before the native ABI stabilizes.

text: Honor MODULE_LICENSE and GPL-only symbol semantics unchanged for inherited Linux modules under the fork.
rationale: Inherited drivers must behave identically or hardware support silently changes legal status.

text: Ensure immutable content-addressed packages preserve LGPL relinking rights (dynamic linking or shipped object files) for LGPL libraries such as glibc and Wine.
rationale: LGPL section 6 requires that users can substitute a modified library and immutable packaging must not remove that ability.

text: Decide whether GPLv3 components (GRUB, coreutils, bash, gnupg) may appear in the boot chain or base image and, if so, provide GPLv3 Installation Information via user-enrollable Secure Boot keys.
rationale: Measured and secure boot combined with GPLv3 triggers anti-tivoization obligations that the boot design must satisfy.

text: Plan the shim submission and Microsoft UEFI CA signing process including the legal entity that applies, review-board requirements and re-signing on each shim change.
rationale: Booting on retail hardware with Secure Boot enabled is impossible for a public alpha without a signed shim.

text: Decide whether the Linux personality userland is built from source or redistributes an existing distribution's binaries, and settle the resulting trademark and license obligations.
rationale: Redistributing another distribution's packages inherits its trademark rules and source-offer duties.

text: Exclude GPLv2-incompatible filesystems such as CDDL ZFS from in-kernel use in the filesystem choice ADR.
rationale: An otherwise attractive storage backend would make the kernel undistributable.

text: Confine the Wasm runtime (Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception for Wasmtime) to userspace and forbid in-kernel Wasm execution on license grounds.
rationale: The runtime's license is GPLv2-incompatible so any kernel-side embedding is blocked regardless of technical merit.

text: Adopt a clean-room policy for the Windows personality mirroring Wine's rules: no disassembly of Microsoft binaries, exclusion of contributors exposed to leaked Windows source, and no bundling of Microsoft redistributables or fonts.
rationale: Any taint in the Win32 reimplementation exposes the whole project to copyright claims.

text: Define a policy that compatibility work never circumvents DRM or anti-tamper protections and document DMCA 1201 and EU equivalent exposure.
rationale: Gaming compatibility attracts circumvention pressure and a single incident can end the project legally.

text: Decide the approach to anti-cheat vendors (EAC, BattlEye) including required legal agreements and whether the project entity is able to sign them.
rationale: Meaningful Windows gaming compatibility depends on vendor cooperation that only a legal entity can obtain.

text: Define an upstream-contribution policy for Wine, Proton, DXVK and VKD3D: no long-lived Wine fork, upstream-first patches, and LGPL source provision for any modified Wine builds shipped.
rationale: Forking Wine is unsustainable and LGPL compliance for shipped builds is mandatory.

text: Establish a patent-encumbered codec policy (H.264, HEVC, AAC, Dolby) covering software decoders, hardware passthrough and jurisdiction-dependent packaging.
rationale: A desktop that cannot play common media is unusable, but shipping encumbered decoders without a policy creates royalty exposure.

text: Audit and record licenses of all shipped fonts and use metric-compatible substitutes for Windows core fonts.
rationale: Fonts are frequently non-redistributable and the Windows personality tempts bundling Microsoft fonts.

text: Run a trademark clearance search for the project name across major jurisdictions and register word and logo marks before any public release.
rationale: Renaming after a public alpha destroys recognition and invites squatting.

text: Publish a trademark usage policy for derivatives, spins, merchandise and compatible-with claims modeled on Debian, Fedora and Rust policies.
rationale: Without a policy the mark either cannot be enforced or blocks legitimate community use.

text: Decide whether Linux appears in any product naming and, if so, obtain the Linux Mark Institute sublicense.
rationale: Linux is a registered trademark and Linux-derived is a claim that must be worded carefully.

text: Define rules for referring to Windows, Steam, Proton and other third-party marks in compatibility documentation and marketing.
rationale: Compatibility claims are the most trademark-sensitive statements the project will make.

text: Register the project's domains, package repository namespace, code-hosting organisation and social handles under the legal entity rather than an individual.
rationale: Infrastructure owned by one person is a single point of failure for a multi-year project.

text: Adopt DCO Signed-off-by for kernel contributions and decide between DCO and a non-assignment CLA for userspace, recorded as an ADR.
rationale: Contribution provenance must be captured from the first commit because it cannot be reconstructed later.

text: Enforce Signed-off-by and verified commit signatures in CI on every merged commit.
rationale: Provenance policy is worthless unless mechanically enforced.

text: Define an AI-assisted contribution policy covering disclosure, provenance, license compatibility of generated code and reviewer responsibility.
rationale: The project is tracked and partly implemented by AI agents, and upstream Linux and others are adopting such rules that the fork must interoperate with.

text: Decide the copyright holder model (contributors retain copyright versus assignment to an entity) and whether any relicensing clause exists.
rationale: This determines whether license corrections are ever possible and whether external contributors will participate.

text: Decide whether and when to form a legal entity (foundation, fiscal sponsor or company) able to hold trademarks and signing keys and to sign vendor agreements.
rationale: Shim signing, anti-cheat agreements, OIN membership and donations all require a counterparty.

text: Which jurisdiction should the legal entity be in, considering export controls, GDPR, trademark cost and tax treatment of donations?
rationale: Jurisdiction shapes every later compliance obligation and is expensive to change.

text: File the publicly-available encryption source notification under EAR 742.15(b) and document export-control classification for releases containing disk encryption and TLS.
rationale: Public binary distribution of cryptography from or through the US requires the notice to use the open-source exception.

text: Write a privacy policy and data-handling design for crash reporting, hardware compatibility submissions and any telemetry, defaulting to opt-in and GDPR-compliant.
rationale: Crash reporting and a hardware database are V3 requirements that collect personal data.

text: Publish package repository terms: developer agreement, content policy, malware removal and DMCA notice and counter-notice process.
rationale: Hosting third-party packages makes the project an intermediary with legal duties.

text: Define root signing key custody: key ceremony, HSM storage, release-signing quorum, rotation and revocation, and which governance roles hold them.
rationale: Signing infrastructure is only as trustworthy as the governance of who can sign.

text: Establish a security response process: SECURITY.md, coordinated-disclosure embargo policy, CNA application and linux-distros list participation once publicly distributed.
rationale: A kernel fork owns CVE response and needs embargoed access to upstream fixes.

text: Decide whether to run a bug bounty program and how it is funded.
rationale: A public beta benefits from external researchers but a bounty is a legal and financial commitment.

text: Adopt an upstream-first policy for the Linux-derived hardware layer: driver and subsystem fixes go to upstream Linux before or alongside the fork.
rationale: It keeps the divergence surface small and preserves goodwill needed when adapting upstream changes.

text: Maintain a divergence ledger classifying every fork patch as upstream-candidate, fork-only or temporary, with rebase status, exposed as a generated report.
rationale: Controlled divergence is only controlled if every patch is accounted for.

text: Decide the upstream base to track (LTS versus mainline), rebase cadence, and the measurable criteria that trigger the Phase D transition to controlled divergence.
rationale: The kernel evolution phases need objective triggers rather than judgment calls.

text: Set kernel identity conventions (uname strings, version scheme, bug-report routing) so the fork is never reported to upstream Linux as Linux.
rationale: Misrouted bug reports damage the upstream relationship and confuse users.

text: Define the relationship with Rust-for-Linux: contribute reusable abstractions upstream and set a policy for Rust toolchain version pinning relative to upstream's minimum.
rationale: Diverging Rust kernel infrastructure would forfeit the largest source of future safe-abstraction work.

text: Define upstream engagement policies with freedesktop.org projects (Wayland, PipeWire, xdg portals), Mesa and systemd for the Linux personality.
rationale: Linux compatibility is a product and its components have upstreams that must not be forked casually.

text: Critical upstream kernel CVE fixes land in a released fork generation within a fixed SLA, measured continuously and published.
rationale: Owning CVE response is the permanent cost of forking and must be measurable.

text: Zero unclassified fork patches and full SBOM coverage are required at every milestone gate.
rationale: Compliance debt compounds and gates are the only enforcement point.

text: Define the RFC process: stages, templates, discussion venues, final-comment period, decision authority and timeboxes.
rationale: Architecture decisions spanning decades need a repeatable, recorded process from V0.

text: Define the ADR template and lifecycle (proposed, accepted, superseded, deprecated) with a mandatory options-considered section and linkage to task IDs.
rationale: ADR tasks are a planning assumption but their format and lifecycle are undefined.

text: Institute heightened change control for Layer 1 native kernel ABI changes: mandatory RFC, compatibility review, and an ABI freeze policy per milestone.
rationale: Kernel ABI mistakes are the hardest to fix and need a stricter process than SDK changes.

text: Publish a deprecation policy per stability layer specifying notice periods and minimum supported overlap for Layer 2 interfaces.
rationale: Strong versioning is meaningless without a stated removal schedule.

text: Publish a 1.0 stability contract stating which ABIs and interfaces are frozen, the support lifecycle, and what constitutes a breaking change.
rationale: A stable release is a promise and the promise must be written down.

text: Decide the versioning scheme for OS releases, kernel, SDK and interfaces (semver for interfaces, generation counters for systems, channel names).
rationale: Packages, generations and interface negotiation all need one coherent versioning vocabulary.

text: Define the release support lifecycle: number of supported releases, security-only phase length and EOL communication.
rationale: Users of a beta need to know how long a release receives fixes.

text: Adopt a governance charter: decision model (BDFL, council or foundation TSC), maintainer appointment and removal, voting and conflict resolution.
rationale: External contributors will not invest without knowing how decisions are made.

text: Maintain a MAINTAINERS/CODEOWNERS mapping per workstream with review requirements enforced by the forge.
rationale: Thirty workstreams need explicit ownership for reviews and gate sign-off.

text: Adopt a Code of Conduct with a named enforcement body and escalation path before the repository opens to external contributors.
rationale: Public projects without one lose contributors at the first incident.

text: Publish CONTRIBUTING guidance covering commit conventions, review expectations, response-time targets and how to propose or modify tasks in the tracking repository.
rationale: The Markdown task repository is the coordination surface and needs rules for humans and agents alike.

text: Define a vendor influence and conflict-of-interest policy for hardware vendors, game platforms and sponsors.
rationale: Target-hardware selection and gaming partnerships create obvious capture risks.

text: Decide the funding model (donations, sponsorship tiers, fiscal sponsor) and publish transparent finances.
rationale: Hardware, CI capacity and signing infrastructure cost money before V2.

text: Define milestone gate governance: who approves gate exit, evidence required, and how milestones are re-scoped or tasks dropped.
rationale: Gates and exit criteria exist as files but need an owner and a process to be meaningful.

text: Define the research program process: timeboxed spikes, evaluation against the litmus test, graduation to ADR, and kill criteria.
rationale: The inspiration list becomes wasted effort without a way to convert research into decisions.

text: Stand up community infrastructure (issue tracker, forum, chat, mailing lists) with a moderation policy and archive guarantees.
rationale: Public alpha users need somewhere to report and discuss.

text: Publish an issue triage policy with labels, severity definitions, response targets and stale handling.
rationale: A public tracker without triage rules becomes noise within weeks.

text: Decide the documentation license (CC-BY-SA, CC-BY or CC0) and the terms for translation contributions.
rationale: Documentation is a V3 requirement and translations are contributions with their own licensing.

text: License the task-tracking and decisions repository itself and state the license of ADR content.
rationale: The planning corpus will be read and forked by others and needs clear terms from the start.

text: Publish a downstream and derivative-distribution policy covering rebranding requirements, unofficial builds and use of the official package repository.
rationale: Beta-stage spins will appear and need rules that protect users and the mark.

text: Define package repository curation governance: review criteria, approval roles, appeals, and free/non-free channel separation with explicit user consent for non-free.
rationale: Shipping Steam or proprietary drivers requires a non-free channel with clear consent.

text: Assess EU Accessibility Act obligations for operating systems and plan the conformity evidence required at 1.0.
rationale: The Act explicitly covers consumer operating systems and applies to products placed on the EU market.

text: Assess EU Cyber Resilience Act obligations (open-source steward versus manufacturer status, vulnerability handling, SBOM, update duration) and plan compliance for 1.0.
rationale: A publicly distributed OS with digital elements falls under the Act's reporting and update duties.

text: Define a vendor NDA policy so hardware documentation under NDA can inform but never be reproduced in open-source drivers.
rationale: Target-hardware enablement will involve NDA material that must not taint the codebase.

text: Decide on Open Invention Network membership and a defensive patent pledge for the project entity.
rationale: Patent exposure grows with public distribution and OIN membership is the standard mitigation for Linux-derived systems.

text: Decide the license for the benchmark dataset and hardware compatibility database (CC0 or ODbL).
rationale: Both are published community datasets and need reuse terms.

text: Adopt a maintainer succession and continuity plan covering key escrow, admin access and bus factor for critical workstreams.
rationale: A multi-year project must survive the loss of any single maintainer.

text: Operate a public transparency log for package and release signing so signing actions are independently auditable.
rationale: Users of a stable release need evidence that the signing keys were not misused.

text: Does placing NT-object or PE-loading emulation in the GPLv2 kernel create license conflicts with LGPL Wine components, or must all Win32 emulation remain in userspace?
rationale: The answer constrains the Windows personality architecture before implementation starts.

text: Do not pursue formal security certifications (Common Criteria, FIPS 140) for 1.0.
rationale: Certification cost and process would divert effort from the stability contract without benefiting the target audience.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Decide the repository topology (single monorepo containing kernel fork, native userspace, SDK and tooling vs. multiple repositories with a pinned manifest) and record it as an ADR before any second repository is created.
rationale: Every CI, versioning, bisection and release-promotion design downstream depends on whether a commit identifies the whole system or only one part of it.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Decide the top-level build orchestrator for a mixed C+Rust kernel and Rust-first userspace (Kbuild driven by Cargo workspaces, Bazel/Buck2, or a derivation-based builder aligned with the content-addressed store) and record trade-offs as an ADR.
rationale: The build orchestrator determines whether reproducibility, remote caching and hermeticity are properties of the system or bolt-ons that fight it for years.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Standardise on LLVM/Clang as the sole C compiler for the kernel fork and document GCC kernel builds as unsupported.
rationale: Rust-in-kernel requires bindgen against libclang and mixing GCC-built C with rustc-built Rust creates ABI and sanitizer mismatches that double the test matrix.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Define a pinned Rust toolchain policy for kernel code: exact rustc version, the allowed set of unstable features, an upgrade cadence tied to upstream Rust-for-Linux, and a CI job that builds with the next candidate toolchain.
rationale: Kernel Rust still depends on unstable features and an unmanaged toolchain bump can break the build for every contributor at once.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Create and maintain a dedicated Rust target triple for native userspace (e.g. x86_64-unknown-jakeos) with a std/alloc port over the native ABI, initially as a custom JSON target and later proposed for tier-3 upstream inclusion.
rationale: Native applications must not be compiled as Linux binaries or the native ABI firewall in §3 is silently violated by the toolchain itself.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Deliver a cross-compilation bootstrap from a Linux host that produces a bootable image, then achieve self-hosted builds of the complete system on JakeOS by V1.
rationale: §61 makes daily-driving mandatory and developers cannot daily-drive an OS they must leave to rebuild.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Make every build run inside a hermetic sandbox with pinned, content-addressed inputs and no network access after dependency fetch, using the native environment primitive (§35) once it exists and a Linux-host equivalent before then.
rationale: Reproducible builds and trustworthy provenance are impossible if builds can read ambient host state.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Achieve bit-for-bit reproducible builds for the kernel, all native packages, the SDK and complete system generation images, verified by at least two independent rebuilders per release.
rationale: Content-addressed package identity (§27) and supply-chain trust are meaningless if the same source yields different bytes.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Eliminate non-determinism sources in Rust and C output (build paths, timestamps, codegen-units, incremental compilation, hash seeds, embedded absolute paths) and add a CI job that builds twice and diffs artifacts on every merge.
rationale: Reproducibility regresses one commit at a time and only a continuous double-build check prevents rediscovering the problem at release.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Generate an SBOM and signed build provenance attestation (SLSA-style) for every release artifact, covering vendored crates, inherited Linux sources and redistributed firmware blobs.
rationale: A 1.0 OS is a supply-chain root for its users and must be able to answer which sources produced which shipped bytes.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Define the third-party dependency policy: committed lockfiles, a vendored source mirror for all crates and C dependencies, cargo-deny licence and advisory checks in CI, and a review requirement for new dependencies.
rationale: Hermetic builds need offline sources and an OS must not ship a crate it cannot audit or rebuild if crates.io disappears.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Maintain kernel configuration as a base defconfig plus per-target fragments (QEMU minimal, QEMU desktop, each reference machine) with a CI check that every fragment still builds and boots.
rationale: Uncontrolled CONFIG drift is the most common way a kernel fork breaks hardware it previously supported.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Decide whether IDL-generated code is committed or generated at build time, and in either case add a CI check that generator output is deterministic and matches the checked-in interface definitions.
rationale: Typed IPC across a multi-repo or multi-language ecosystem breaks silently when generated stubs drift from their IDL.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Add a native kernel ABI snapshot check to CI that diffs syscall surface, object types and message layouts against a golden snapshot and fails unless the change is linked to an approved ADR.
rationale: §65 calls the ABI the most permanent decision, so accidental ABI changes must be mechanically impossible rather than caught in review.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Build an SDK-level compatibility suite that compiles applications against SDK version N and runs them on system generation N+1 (and vice versa where promised) to enforce the Layer 2 versioning rules of §66.
rationale: Interface versioning is only real if something tests old binaries against new platforms on every merge.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Deploy a shared content-addressed remote build cache (compiler cache plus artifact cache) usable by CI and by developers, with cache hits verified against reproducible outputs.
rationale: A kernel plus userspace plus compatibility layers is too large to rebuild from scratch on every CI run without making pre-merge feedback unusably slow.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Set and track build-time budgets: incremental kernel rebuild under 2 minutes, incremental native userspace rebuild under 1 minute, full clean CI build under 30 minutes on the reference runner.
rationale: Build latency directly determines contributor throughput and whether people run tests before pushing.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Define build profiles (debug with lockdep/KASAN/KCSAN/UBSAN/KFENCE and Rust debug assertions, release with LTO and stripped symbols, and a symbols-preserved release variant) and run the debug profile in nightly CI.
rationale: Memory-safety bugs in inherited C and unsafe Rust are only caught if sanitized kernels are actually booted and exercised regularly.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Decide the linker (lld vs. mold), LTO scope and PGO policy for kernel and userspace, and measure their effect on the §54 benchmarks before adopting them.
rationale: Link-time choices affect binary size, startup latency and reproducibility, and PGO in particular threatens bit-for-bit builds.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Keep an ARM64 kernel and userspace cross-build compiling in CI (boot not required) even though ARM64 is not a supported platform before 1.0.
rationale: §38 forbids fossilising on x86-64 and a build that has silently become x86-only is far harder to un-break later than one that never compiles elsewhere.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Distribute versioned developer toolchains (rustc target, IDL compiler, image tools, QEMU harness) as immutable packages installable on Linux and macOS hosts and natively on JakeOS with a single toolchain manager command.
rationale: Third-party developers in V3 cannot be expected to reproduce the project's build environment by hand.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Decide the CI platform with the explicit requirement of self-hosted bare-metal runners exposing KVM and connected to the hardware lab, and treat hosted runners as acceptable only for lint and unit tests.
rationale: Boot, graphics, performance and hardware testing all need nested virtualisation or real devices that hosted CI cannot provide.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Manage all CI and lab infrastructure as code with documented disaster recovery so the entire build and test pipeline can be recreated from the repository plus backups.
rationale: A years-long project will lose machines, accounts and people, and unrecoverable CI is a project-ending risk.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Structure CI into tiers: pre-merge (lint, unit, QEMU smoke boot under 15 minutes), post-merge (full QEMU matrix), nightly (sanitizers, fuzzing, performance, hardware lab) and release qualification.
rationale: A single monolithic pipeline is either too slow to gate merges or too shallow to catch regressions.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Enforce a merge queue on the main branch so every landed commit was tested against the exact tree it landed on, with no direct pushes.
rationale: Bisection and the generated roll-up progress tables assume main is always green and every commit is attributable to a passing run.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Define the QEMU/KVM test matrix: q35 machine, OVMF with and without Secure Boot, TPM emulation, virtio block/net/gpu/input/sound, CPU counts of 1, 2, 8 and 64, memory from 512 MB to 64 GB, and multi-node NUMA topologies.
rationale: Scheduling, memory-object locality and boot paths behave differently across these axes and only a declared matrix makes coverage auditable.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Build a boot test harness that drives QEMU and lab machines to a boot-complete marker over serial, detects kernel panics and Rust panics, enforces timeouts, and exercises reboot, kexec and generation-selection cycles.
rationale: The kernel fork is the foundation and a boot regression must be detected within one CI cycle, not by a developer noticing.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Adopt KUnit plus Rust kernel unit tests and doctests for all native primitives, run on every pre-merge build under QEMU.
rationale: Capability derivation, channel semantics and operation lifecycles need fast in-kernel unit coverage before integration tests are viable.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Build a guest-side test agent for the native userspace image that runs test components, streams structured results out over virtio-serial or vsock, and maps test failures to task IDs from the Markdown repository.
rationale: Integration tests of components, channels and capabilities must run inside the booted OS and report machine-readable results to CI.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Produce reproducible test images per milestone (minimal execution-model image for V0, desktop image from V0.5) via a single image builder shared with release engineering.
rationale: Test images that diverge from shipped images test the wrong thing.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Integrate Linux compatibility conformance suites (LTP, glibc tests, selected syzkaller Linux descriptions in differential mode against upstream Linux, and an application smoke corpus) into nightly CI for the Linux personality.
rationale: §56.3 says compatibility is a product, and a product needs a regression suite that measures behavioural divergence from real Linux.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Integrate the Wine conformance test suite and a curated Windows application and game smoke corpus into nightly CI on GPU-equipped lab machines.
rationale: Windows gaming is a major product objective in §48 and regressions there are invisible to QEMU-only testing.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Build the end-to-end GUI test harness on semantic interfaces (§42) and the accessibility tree rather than pixel or coordinate scripting, with pixel-based golden-image tests reserved for compositor rendering correctness.
rationale: The project's own principle is that semantic interfaces beat GUI scraping, and dogfooding that in the test harness proves the interfaces are complete.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Provide a software-rendered and virtio-gpu compositor path so the desktop stack can be tested headlessly in QEMU, with golden-image comparison tolerant of documented rasterisation differences.
rationale: Without a GPU-less rendering path every UI change needs physical hardware and desktop testing becomes a bottleneck.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Publish a flaky-test policy: automatic quarantine after a defined flake rate, at most one retry, a time-boxed deflake obligation on the owning workstream, and quarantine expiry that deletes or fixes the test.
rationale: Unmanaged flakes erode trust in CI until people merge on red, which destroys the value of every other gate.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Deploy a test results database and dashboard (KernelCI-style) recording per-commit, per-configuration and per-machine outcomes with history, flake rate and duration trends.
rationale: Years of results across a hardware matrix cannot be understood from individual CI logs.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Measure code coverage for kernel (kcov/gcov and Rust coverage) and userspace, and set minimum coverage gates for capability enforcement, ABI entry points and IDL-generated code paths.
rationale: Security-critical paths need evidence of exercise, not assumptions.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Enforce static analysis gates in pre-merge CI: rustfmt and clippy with warnings denied, sparse and smatch for inherited C, cargo-deny, an adapted checkpatch, and Miri for unsafe userspace Rust where feasible.
rationale: Style and lint disagreements are cheapest to settle mechanically at the first commit.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Track every unsafe block in native code with a required SAFETY comment, a CI-generated unsafe inventory per crate, and a trend line so unsafe surface area is a reviewed metric.
rationale: §51 requires unsafe authority to be minimised and isolated, which needs measurement to be enforceable.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Build an upstream-tracking bot that attempts merges of each upstream Linux stable and mainline tag into the fork, reports conflicts by subsystem, and runs the boot matrix on the result.
rationale: §6 Phase D adaptation of upstream changes needs continuous visibility of divergence cost or merges stop happening.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Automate CVE ingestion: match upstream Linux security fixes against the forked tree, flag ones touching diverged code, and open tracked tasks with deadlines defined by the security response policy.
rationale: §56.4 makes CVE response a permanent owned cost and manual tracking against a diverging tree will miss fixes.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Adapt syzkaller to the native ABI: syzlang descriptions for object handles, typed channels, operations and memory objects, a capability-aware executor that can obtain and derive capabilities, and a custom program generator that understands handle ownership transfer.
rationale: Stock syzkaller cannot express typed, capability-scoped calls and the native ABI is exactly where novel kernel bugs will live.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Run continuous fuzzing infrastructure (syzbot-like) with crash deduplication, reproducer minimisation, automatic bisection and automatic task filing into the Markdown repository.
rationale: Fuzzing without triage automation produces a crash backlog nobody works.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Have the IDL compiler emit fuzz harnesses and structure-aware mutators for every interface and wire format it generates.
rationale: Typed IPC boundaries are the trust boundaries between components and each one must be fuzzed for free rather than by hand.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Fuzz all userspace parsers of untrusted input (package manifests, environment.yaml, fonts, images, capability serialisation, personality PE/ELF loaders) with cargo-fuzz corpora maintained in the repository.
rationale: Parsers are the historical entry point for most desktop OS exploits.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Write property-based and model-based tests for capability invariants (attenuation never widens authority, revocation is complete and observable, transfer preserves type) and evaluate Kani or a TLA+ model of the derivation core.
rationale: §9 rests entirely on these invariants holding and example-based tests cannot demonstrate absence of escalation paths.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Build a fault-injection framework that kills userspace services (compositor, audio, network, device management) and injects kernel allocation and I/O failures during test runs to verify §32 restart and rebind semantics.
rationale: Recovery that is never exercised in CI will not work when it matters.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Add resource-leak detection tests using the §24 observability surface: assert zero leaked capabilities, memory objects, channels and tasks after each integration test and after multi-hour soak runs.
rationale: Leaked kernel objects in a long-lived desktop session are the most common cause of gradual degradation.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Run multi-day soak tests on lab hardware covering suspend/resume cycles, generation accumulation, repeated application launches and long compositor uptime, with memory and latency trend alerts.
rationale: Beta users will run the system for weeks and CI otherwise only tests minutes.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Stand up a dedicated performance CI fleet of quiet bare-metal machines with fixed CPU frequency, disabled turbo and SMT policies documented, isolated from other CI load.
rationale: Microsecond-scale IPC and component-creation targets cannot be measured on shared or virtualised runners.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Store all benchmark results in a time-series database with change-point detection, noise-calibrated thresholds and automatic bisection to the offending commit.
rationale: §54 demands every claim have a benchmark and a benchmark that nobody watches cannot catch regressions.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Define a blocking performance gate: a regression beyond the calibrated noise band on tier-one benchmarks (IPC round trip, component creation, app startup, input-to-photon) blocks merge unless an ADR-linked exception is recorded.
rationale: Performance is a stated architectural claim and must be protected with the same rigour as correctness.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Build an input-to-photon latency measurement rig (HID injection plus photodiode or high-speed capture) attached to lab machines and report it as a tracked benchmark.
rationale: §54 lists GUI input-to-photon latency but it cannot be measured in software alone.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Instrument lab machines with external power meters and battery-drain cycles to produce the §54 energy benchmarks per release.
rationale: Energy claims for laptops are unverifiable from software counters alone.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Establish a physical hardware lab holding the §62 reference machines with remote power control, network boot, serial or USB-debug consoles, HDMI/DisplayPort capture, USB device switching, programmable HID input, and Wi-Fi and Bluetooth peer devices.
rationale: GPU, suspend, wireless and peripheral behaviour cannot be validated in QEMU and §55 forbids destabilising hardware support.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Deploy lab scheduling software (LAVA-like or custom) that reserves machines, flashes images, runs jobs and returns results to CI, with automatic recovery of an unbootable machine via firmware boot-order fallback to a known-good generation.
rationale: Without automation the lab becomes a manual queue that CI cannot depend on.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Run GPU conformance (Vulkan CTS, dEQP) and compositor tests nightly on AMD, Intel and NVIDIA lab machines and track pass rates per driver generation.
rationale: §56.1 names GPU drivers the hardest hardware problem and regressions must be caught per vendor.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Automate suspend/resume, hibernate and lid/dock event testing with RTC wake across hundreds of cycles on each laptop reference machine.
rationale: Suspend regressions are the most common laptop failure and appear only under repetition.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Maintain a firmware version matrix for lab machines and test system behaviour before and after vendor firmware updates.
rationale: Firmware changes silently alter ACPI, TPM and boot behaviour that the boot and security stacks depend on.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Define hardware support tiers (Tier 1 CI-gated in the lab, Tier 2 nightly or periodic, Tier 3 community-reported) and make the tier the unit of the hardware compatibility database.
rationale: §62 deliberately constrains target hardware and users need to know what tier a machine actually gets.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Ship a user-runnable hardware conformance tool that executes the compatibility suite on an arbitrary machine and submits anonymised, consented results to the compatibility database.
rationale: A public alpha will meet hardware the lab never will and the project needs structured reports instead of forum threads.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Build the release artifact pipeline: build once, sign, publish generation images, installer media, package repository and SDK, then promote the identical artifacts through nightly, testing and stable channels without rebuilding.
rationale: Rebuilding per channel invalidates the testing that justified promotion.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Automate release qualification as a checklist evaluated by CI: all gates green, reproducibility verified, Tier 1 hardware pass, no unresolved performance regressions, upgrade and rollback chain tests passed.
rationale: Human-run release checklists drift and a 1.0 promise requires the gate to be mechanical.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Test upgrade paths automatically: generation N to N+1 and rollback, plus a long chain from the oldest supported release to current, on both QEMU and lab hardware.
rationale: §30 makes rollback first-class and only continuous upgrade testing keeps that guarantee true across releases.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Run the installer automatically in QEMU across disk layouts (fresh UEFI, encrypted, dual-boot alongside Windows, existing data preservation) with Secure Boot enabled and disabled.
rationale: The installer is the first thing every alpha user runs and its failures are the most public.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Collect kernel crash artifacts in CI and in the field (pstore/kdump, symbolised Rust panic backtraces) and operate a debug symbol server (debuginfod-style) for every released build.
rationale: Stripped release builds without symbol retrieval make crash reports from §63 useless.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Provide a single developer command that builds, boots the result in QEMU and runs the same test harness CI uses, with a target of under 30 minutes from fresh clone to a booted QEMU image on a standard Linux host.
rationale: Contributor onboarding time is the primary constraint on the community §56.5 says the project cannot succeed without.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Migrate CI runners themselves to run on JakeOS by V2 so the build and test infrastructure is dogfooded alongside the desktop.
rationale: Self-hosting the infrastructure exposes server-shaped gaps (unattended operation, remote management) that desktop dogfooding never will.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Automate dependency update proposals (crates, C libraries, firmware, QEMU, upstream Linux) as CI-validated changes with a documented review cadence.
rationale: Manual dependency tracking across a kernel fork and a Rust ecosystem falls behind within months.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Run licence compliance scanning in CI covering GPLv2 obligations for kernel code, crate licences, firmware redistribution terms and the Windows/Linux test corpus, with an ADR fixing the userspace licence choice.
rationale: Licence violations discovered at public alpha would block distribution of every artifact.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Assemble a legally reviewed test corpus of Linux applications, Windows applications and games, fonts, images and documents that CI is permitted to redistribute to runners.
rationale: Compatibility and parser testing need real inputs and most real inputs carry licences that forbid casual redistribution.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Mirror all upstream sources (Linux, crates, firmware, Wine, toolchain) in project-controlled storage keyed by content hash.
rationale: Reproducing a release years later requires the inputs to still exist.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Test nested virtualisation and the retained KVM path in CI so JakeOS can host VMs, including running its own test harness inside a guest.
rationale: KVM is listed as preserved in §5 and preservation claims need tests.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Track kernel image size, initial image size and boot time to first frame as budgeted metrics with regression alerts.
rationale: Cheap isolation and fast startup claims degrade invisibly through bloat unless size and boot time are watched.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Do not build or maintain a custom compiler or forked LLVM; carry only minimal, upstream-bound patches against rustc and LLVM.
rationale: Compiler maintenance would consume the engineering budget §56.4 already commits to kernel maintenance.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Do not support building the OS from Windows or macOS hosts natively before 1.0; provide a containerised Linux build environment for those hosts instead.
rationale: Every additional host platform multiplies toolchain and reproducibility work for little contributor gain before a public release.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Decide how the fork responds when upstream Linux raises its minimum Rust version or stabilises features the fork's Rust code depends on, including whether to track upstream's minimum or pin independently.
rationale: Diverging toolchain requirements from upstream make Phase D driver adaptation progressively more expensive.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Investigate using native components and resource domains as the isolation unit for parallel test execution (one component per test) once the primitives are stable.
rationale: Using the OS's own cheap isolation for its test harness is both a performance win and a continuous proof that §10 creation cost targets hold.

lens: Build, toolchain, CI and test infrastructure
text: Build documentation and ADR CI: generate interface reference docs from IDL, check ADR cross-links and task ID references, and fail on broken links or unparseable task templates.
rationale: The Markdown repository is the source of truth for years of progress and its parseability must be enforced like code.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Publish a written threat model naming adversaries (malicious native app, compromised component, compromised compatibility app, local unprivileged user, evil-maid with device off, evil-maid with device suspended, malicious DMA peripheral, network attacker, supply-chain attacker), protected assets, and trust boundaries, and require every CAP/SEC/BOOT ADR to cite which threats it addresses.
rationale: The baseline asserts 'no ambient authority' but never says what the system defends against, so 1.0 security claims cannot be evaluated or audited without it.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide UEFI-only boot with no legacy BIOS/CSM support for 1.0.
rationale: Secure Boot, measured boot and a signed generation chain are only coherent on UEFI, and supporting CSM doubles bootloader and installer test surface.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: ADR: adopt an existing UEFI bootloader (systemd-boot or GRUB) versus writing a native Rust UEFI bootloader that understands generations and the content-addressed store directly.
rationale: Generation selection, boot counting and PCR measurement policy all depend on this choice, and §57 forbids rewriting mature pieces without a demonstrated benefit.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: ADR: whether each generation boots as a single signed Unified Kernel Image (kernel + early userspace + command line in one PE) or as separately verified components.
rationale: A single signed image is what makes Secure Boot signing and PCR prediction tractable; the format must be fixed before the generation store layout is.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Define a stable on-disk boot-entry format that maps a bootloader menu entry to a generation ID, its kernel image, its verified system-store root hash and its signed manifest.
rationale: The bootloader and the package/generation system are built by different workstreams and need a fixed contract that survives both bootloader and store evolution.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: ADR: early userspace strategy — a native init component that runs before the root store is unlocked, versus reusing a Linux initramfs and systemd for early boot with the native world starting afterwards.
rationale: Disk unlock, verity setup and service supervision all live in early boot, and reusing systemd here risks fossilizing Linux semantics into the native boot path.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Build a native init and service supervisor that starts system services as components with declared capabilities, dependency-ordered startup, restart policies and readiness signalling, replacing systemd for the native world.
rationale: §32 requires restartable services but nothing in the baseline owns starting, ordering or supervising them.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Sign every system generation manifest with a release key and have the bootloader verify the manifest before offering or booting the generation.
rationale: Without a signed manifest the immutable generation model has no root of trust and rollback can be abused to boot tampered system state.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Apply block- or file-level verity (dm-verity/fs-verity style) to the immutable system store with its root hash carried in the signed generation manifest, completing the chain from firmware to userspace binaries.
rationale: §26 asks for checksums but a checksum without a signed root is integrity, not authenticity; 1.0 needs a verifiable chain of trust.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Implement boot counting and automatic fallback: the bootloader tracks boot attempts per generation, marks a generation bad after N failures, and boots the last known-good generation without user action.
rationale: §30 says 'if boot fails, boot the previous generation' but does not define how failure is detected or how fallback happens unattended.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide the definition of 'boot succeeded' used to clear the boot counter (e.g. session manager reached login, or the user authenticated) and which component is authorised to report it.
rationale: Too early a definition lets a broken desktop mark itself good; too late one makes headless and recovery boots impossible.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Make bootloader and ESP updates atomic using a dual-slot or write-then-rename scheme with a tested rollback of the bootloader itself.
rationale: An interrupted bootloader update is the one failure generations cannot roll back from.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Treat the kernel command line as part of the signed generation, not user-editable at boot time outside developer mode.
rationale: An editable command line (init=/bin/sh, lockdown=off) defeats Secure Boot and measured boot.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Ship a documented developer mode that lets a machine owner enrol their own Secure Boot keys, boot self-built kernels and disable lockdown, with a persistent, non-suppressible on-screen indicator while active.
rationale: V1 requires developers to build the OS on the OS, which is impossible if only release-signed kernels boot, but silently unlocked machines must be visibly distinguishable.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide the Secure Boot distribution strategy: ship via shim signed by the Microsoft third-party UEFI CA, require users to enrol the project's own PK/KEK/db keys, or support both.
rationale: Most target hardware ships with only Microsoft keys, so this decision determines whether ordinary users can boot with Secure Boot on at all.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: If shim is chosen, run the shim-review submission process and maintain SBAT generation numbers for bootloader and kernel so compromised builds can be revoked without dbx churn.
rationale: Public alpha users need Secure Boot to work out of the box, and revocation is a prerequisite for shipping signed boot components responsibly.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Design and operate the signing key hierarchy: offline root, HSM-backed intermediates for bootloader, kernel, generations and packages, documented rotation cadence and a compromise-response runbook.
rationale: §63 lists 'secure signing' as a requirement but says nothing about custody, rotation or what happens when a key leaks.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Require all kernel-resident code (modules, firmware blobs loaded by drivers) to be signed and rejected when unsigned under Secure Boot.
rationale: Verifying the kernel image while loading unsigned modules leaves the chain of trust open at the most privileged layer.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide how out-of-tree proprietary kernel modules (notably NVIDIA) are handled under Secure Boot: local machine-owner key signing, vendor-signed builds, or unsupported until an open driver suffices.
rationale: §56.1 names NVIDIA as a hard requirement and Secure Boot makes unsigned proprietary modules unloadable.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Enable kernel lockdown (integrity or confidentiality mode) automatically when Secure Boot is active: no unsigned kexec, no raw physical memory access, no unsigned hibernation image, no debugfs writes.
rationale: Secure Boot without lockdown only protects the first boot stage and is trivially bypassed from a compromised root.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Define and maintain a kernel hardening configuration baseline (KASLR, stack protector, kCFI, SMEP/SMAP, IBT, shadow stacks, init_on_alloc/free, hardened usercopy, W^X, randomized freelists) tracked as a checked-in config with CI enforcement.
rationale: The fork inherits Linux's defaults, which are tuned for compatibility rather than a desktop that promises capability-grade security.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Prune the kernel attack surface for the constrained target hardware: disable unused legacy drivers, obsolete filesystems, unneeded protocols and syscalls not required by the native ABI or the Linux personality.
rationale: §62 deliberately limits target hardware, which makes a minimal kernel configuration achievable and removes whole classes of CVEs.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Make the native runtime enable userspace exploit mitigations by default (ASLR, NX, CET shadow stacks and IBT where the CPU supports them, guard pages, hardened allocator) and expose them as component manifest requirements.
rationale: §51 lists language and capability safety but omits the conventional process-level mitigations that still matter for C and unsafe Rust code.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Bound the Linux personality's ambient POSIX authority by the enclosing component's capability set so that a Linux process can never reach a resource its component was not granted, regardless of uid or file mode.
rationale: Compatibility inherits history (§3) but must not become the ambient-authority hole that makes the capability model meaningless in practice.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Model debugger attachment, tracing of another component and reading another component's memory as explicit capabilities rather than same-user or root checks.
rationale: ptrace-style same-uid attach is the classic way ambient authority leaks between sandboxed applications.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide whether TPM 2.0 is a hard hardware requirement for 1.0 or an optional enhancement, and define the degraded behaviour (passphrase-only unlock, no measured boot) on machines without one.
rationale: Measured boot, sealed disk keys and PCR-bound policy all depend on this and it must be reflected in the hardware compatibility database.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Implement measured boot: the bootloader extends the kernel image, command line, generation ID and verity root into TPM PCRs, and the OS ships signed expected PCR policies so a generation update does not invalidate sealed keys.
rationale: Without predictable PCR policy every OS update either locks users out of their disk or forces the disk key to be unsealed with a weak policy.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Expose the TPM to userspace only through a capability-gated TPM service; no ambient /dev/tpm0 or tpm2-tss access for applications.
rationale: A shared TPM device node lets any application exhaust, lock out or misuse platform keys.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Expose the TPM event log and PCR state locally through os inspect, and declare remote attestation (attestation server, enterprise enrolment) a non-goal for 1.0.
rationale: Local inspection satisfies §64's understandability goal while remote attestation would pull an enterprise trust infrastructure into a desktop 1.0.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide the disk-encryption mechanism: reuse LUKS2/dm-crypt under the storage stack versus filesystem-native per-directory encryption versus both, respecting §57's rule against inventing new storage layers.
rationale: V1 developers daily-drive laptops with source code and credentials; encryption must be in place before any lost laptop is possible.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide the encryption layering relative to the content-addressed store and system generations: whether the immutable, publicly known system store is verified-but-unencrypted while user and application data are encrypted, and how deduplication interacts with encryption.
rationale: Encrypting deduplicated content-addressed objects changes both the deduplication ratio and what an attacker learns from ciphertext, so it must be a deliberate choice.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Make the installer encrypt user data by default with an opt-out, not an opt-in.
rationale: Encryption that must be chosen is encryption most users do not have; a security-positioned OS cannot ship unencrypted by default.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Build a pre-boot unlock UI (text at V1, graphical and DPI-aware at V2) supporting passphrase, TPM-sealed key with PIN, recovery key entry, keyboard layout selection and multiple enrolled unlock slots.
rationale: Disk encryption is unusable on a desktop without a reliable unlock experience that works before the compositor exists.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Seal the disk key to TPM PCR state with an optional PIN, and always generate an offline recovery key that the user must save (print, file to removable media) before installation completes; no cloud escrow by default.
rationale: PCR-bound unlock gives passwordless boot on healthy hardware, but firmware updates and motherboard replacement need a guaranteed recovery path.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Re-seal TPM-bound disk keys automatically before and after firmware updates and Secure Boot key changes so a PCR change never strands the user at the recovery-key prompt.
rationale: Firmware updates are the most common cause of TPM unlock failure on shipping OSes.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Support passphrase change and key-slot rotation without re-encrypting the volume, and cryptographic erase (key destruction) as the factory-reset primitive.
rationale: Users must be able to rotate credentials after a compromise and to hand over or dispose of hardware safely.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide whether disk keys are evicted from memory on suspend (requiring re-unlock on resume or suspend-then-hibernate) and whether hibernation is supported at all under lockdown, which requires an encrypted, authenticated hibernation image.
rationale: A suspended laptop with keys in RAM is the dominant realistic attack on encrypted laptops and the baseline lists suspend/resume as a V1 requirement.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Set and track a disk-encryption overhead target (e.g. under 10% sequential and random NVMe throughput loss with AES-NI) in the benchmark suite.
rationale: Encryption by default is only defensible if its performance cost is measured and bounded.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Deliver a firmware update service (LVFS/fwupd-equivalent, UEFI capsule and device firmware) where each firmware update is recorded as a system-history event and, where hardware permits, can be staged and rolled back.
rationale: Firmware updates are a routine security necessity on laptops and the baseline's history model (§31) should cover them like any other state change.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Gate access to UEFI variables and firmware settings behind an explicit capability; no ambient efivarfs.
rationale: Writable efivars from an unprivileged context can brick firmware or alter Secure Boot state.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Ship a permanently resident, signed recovery generation on the ESP that boots without the main store, offering disk unlock, restore to any generation or snapshot, reinstall from network or media, and log collection.
rationale: §63's 'recovery' requirement needs a concrete mechanism that survives corruption of the main store and every normal generation.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Design the integrity-failure user experience: what the user sees and can do when verity verification fails, PCR policy mismatches or a signature is invalid, with a guaranteed path into recovery and never a silent bypass.
rationale: Security failures at boot are inevitable after firmware or hardware changes and a bricked-looking machine will be blamed on the OS.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide the anti-rollback policy: whether booting generations older than a security-fix watermark is blocked, allowed with warning, or allowed only in developer mode, reconciling §30's first-class rollback with downgrade attacks.
rationale: First-class rollback and protection against reintroducing patched vulnerabilities are in direct tension and must be resolved explicitly.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Support dual-boot coexistence: the installer preserves existing ESP entries, the bootloader can chain-load Windows and Linux, and the installer detects BitLocker and refuses to resize protected volumes without warning.
rationale: Enthusiasts and gamers at public alpha will install alongside Windows and destroying their existing OS is unrecoverable reputational damage.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Seed the kernel RNG at boot from TPM, CPU RNG and a bootloader-persisted seed, and provide a trusted time source policy for certificate validation before network time is available.
rationale: Early-boot entropy and clock trust determine whether disk unlock, TLS and signature checks are sound on first boot.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Require IOMMU to be enabled and all DMA-capable devices placed behind it on target hardware, with Thunderbolt/USB4 device authorisation (bolt-style) before PCIe tunnelling is allowed.
rationale: Ownership-transfer and DMA-suitable MemoryObjects (§17) are unsafe against malicious peripherals without hardware DMA protection.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Include Secure Boot custom-key enrolment, TPM 2.0 presence and IOMMU support as hardware-selection criteria for the reference AMD desktop, Intel laptop and AMD laptop.
rationale: §62 constrains target hardware but not by security features, and a reference machine that cannot enrol keys cannot exercise the boot security path.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: ADR: whether a user is a kernel-level identity (uid-like) or purely a userspace identity-service concept mapped to capability roots, and how the Linux personality's uid/gid expectations are derived from it.
rationale: The baseline never says what a 'user' is in a capability system, yet login, home data, secrets and compatibility all hinge on it.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Build an identity service holding local accounts with Argon2id-hashed credentials, exposed only through capability-gated typed interfaces (no readable shadow file) and pluggable authenticator interfaces for future methods.
rationale: Login at V1 needs somewhere to store and verify credentials, and the storage must not be ambient-readable like /etc/shadow-adjacent data has historically been.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Introduce a Session object linking user identity, seat, display and the session's capability root, with lock, unlock, idle, suspend-inhibit and end-of-session as typed interfaces replacing logind's D-Bus API for native software.
rationale: Lock screen, power management, per-session services and compatibility shims all need one authoritative session lifecycle.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Build a native login greeter integrated with the compositor, supporting password login at V1 and fingerprint and FIDO2/passkey login at V3.
rationale: V1 daily driving requires logging in, and later biometric and hardware-key methods are expected on modern laptops.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Implement a compositor-owned lock screen that inhibits all input to applications, hides notification content by policy, locks on idle, lid close and suspend, and cannot be drawn over by any application surface.
rationale: A lock screen is table stakes for a laptop OS and must be enforced by the compositor rather than being an ordinary window.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Guarantee that a compositor crash while locked restarts into the locked state, so §32 recovery never exposes the desktop.
rationale: Compositor-restart recovery is a baseline feature, and crash-to-unlock is a well-known real-world lock screen bypass class.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide the multi-user scope for 1.0: number of local accounts, fast user switching, concurrent graphical sessions, and whether per-user home data is encrypted with per-user keys unlocked at login.
rationale: Each of these multiplies session, encryption and compositor complexity and must be scoped before the identity and storage designs are finalised.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Declare multi-seat, guest sessions, kiosk mode and enterprise directory login (LDAP/AD/Kerberos/SSO) non-goals for 1.0 while requiring the identity service's authenticator interface to remain pluggable.
rationale: These are enterprise and shared-machine features that would divert effort from the single-owner desktop the milestones describe.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Build a privilege-elevation Authorization service that grants scoped capabilities after re-authentication with an audit record, replacing sudo/polkit; native packages contain no setuid binaries.
rationale: Administrative actions (installing drivers, changing system settings) need an authority path that fits the capability model rather than reintroducing root.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Define what 'administrator' versus 'standard user' means in capability terms, which operations require elevation, and that the first account created is an administrator.
rationale: Every settings panel and installer flow needs to know which actions elevate, and the roles must exist before the Settings app is built.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Build a native secrets service in which each application's secrets are capability-scoped objects encrypted under a per-user key unlocked at login, so no application can enumerate or read another application's secrets.
rationale: Today's Secret Service lets any app in the session read every stored password; the capability model should fix this and V1 developers need somewhere to keep tokens.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Provide an SSH agent and Git credential integration backed by the native secrets service, with optional TPM- or FIDO2-resident keys.
rationale: V1 self-hosting requires Git over SSH and developers will otherwise store keys in plain files.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Provide compatibility shims: org.freedesktop.secrets and libsecret for Linux applications, and Windows Credential Manager/DPAPI for the Windows personality, both backed by the native secrets service with per-application scoping.
rationale: Browsers, mail clients and games store credentials through these APIs and must work without granting them a shared password store.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Provide PAM/NSS-equivalent, logind (org.freedesktop.login1) and D-Bus session-bus compatibility for Linux applications, fed from the native identity and Session services so getpwuid, $HOME, XDG_RUNTIME_DIR and session lock/idle signals behave as expected.
rationale: §56.3 says Linux compatibility is a product; desktop applications break in subtle ways without these identity and session facts.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Research whether the OS should act as a WebAuthn platform authenticator (passkey provider) backed by TPM and biometrics, and what browser integration that requires.
rationale: Passkeys are becoming the default login method on the web and a 1.0 desktop without a platform authenticator pushes users to third-party managers.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide the taxonomy of user-mediated grants: which capabilities are granted implicitly by OS choosers (files, contacts), which require a prompt (camera, microphone, location, notifications, persistent background execution), and which are settings-only, with a documented rationale against prompt fatigue.
rationale: §9 assumes grants happen but never says how the user is asked, and prompt design decides whether the capability model is usable or ignored.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Render permission prompts, file choosers and the elevation dialog through a privileged trusted-UI component in compositor-protected surfaces that applications cannot overlay, spoof, resize or synthesise input into.
rationale: A chooser that grants authority (§25) is only as strong as the guarantee that the user, not the application, drove it.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Ship a Settings surface listing every persistent capability grant per application with revocation, expiry and a usage timeline built from the capability audit trail.
rationale: Revocability and inspectability are baseline capability properties (§7) but without a user-facing view they exist only for developers.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Show non-suppressible shell indicators whenever camera, microphone, screen capture or location capabilities are actively exercised, attributing use to the specific application.
rationale: Users expect these indicators from every modern OS and they make capability use visible rather than theoretical.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Decide the default capability bundle for Linux and Windows compatibility applications (which directories, network, devices) and how portal-style requests upgrade it, so legacy applications work without either ambient home access or constant prompting.
rationale: Compatibility apps have no manifest of requested capabilities, and getting this default wrong either breaks them or hollows out the security model.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Run each Windows application in its own component with its own registry and prefix and the compatibility-default capability set, so one compromised game cannot read another application's files or credentials.
rationale: A single shared Wine prefix with user-wide authority would make the Windows personality the weakest point of the whole system.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Define the clipboard authority policy: reads require a user paste gesture or an explicit grant, writes are always allowed, and clipboard history is a privileged shell feature rather than an ambient stream.
rationale: Silent clipboard reading is a common data-exfiltration vector and §41 lists clipboard capabilities without specifying the policy.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Record security-relevant events (authentication failures, elevation grants, capability escalations, Secure Boot state changes, key enrolments) in a tamper-evident, size-bounded audit log viewable via os inspect and the Settings app.
rationale: Observability of capability grants (§24) needs a durable, trustworthy record for incident response, not just live tracing.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Ensure kernel crash dumps and component core dumps never contain disk keys or unlocked secrets: disable kernel dumps under confidentiality lockdown and scrub or encrypt userspace dumps before storage.
rationale: Crash reporting is a V3 requirement (§63) and is a classic channel through which encryption keys and credentials leak.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Do not expose stable hardware or installation identifiers (machine ID, TPM EK, disk serials, MAC addresses) to applications without a capability; provide per-application derived identifiers where needed.
rationale: Ambient device fingerprinting contradicts no-ambient-authority and is trivially available on Linux today via /etc/machine-id and sysfs.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Build the first-boot setup experience (create administrator account, confirm encryption and save the recovery key, privacy and telemetry choices, Secure Boot status explanation).
rationale: Account creation, recovery-key escrow and consent all have to happen exactly once at first boot and no other workstream owns that flow.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Set and track boot-to-login and unlock-to-usable-desktop latency targets (for example under 10 s from firmware handoff to greeter on reference hardware, under 500 ms from unlock to interactive desktop) in the benchmark suite.
rationale: Verity, measured boot and encryption each add boot cost, and §54 demands that every architectural claim carry a benchmark.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
