text: Publish a vulnerability disclosure policy, a security contact, an embargo process and a signed advisory format covering the kernel fork, bootloader, compatibility personalities and the package repository.
rationale: §56.4 acknowledges CVE response as a cost but a public alpha cannot receive reports responsibly without a documented process.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Commission an independent external security audit of the capability kernel, bootloader chain, disk encryption and identity/secrets services before 1.0, with findings tracked as tasks.
rationale: A new security model shipped as stable without outside review is asking users to trust unproven claims.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Publish a user-facing platform security guide stating exactly what the OS protects against (and does not) in each state: powered off, suspended, locked, unlocked, developer mode.
rationale: Users and reviewers will otherwise assume protections the design does not deliver, particularly around suspend and developer mode.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Research whether measured boot and kernel lockdown can provide a platform-integrity signal that Windows anti-cheat vendors would accept in lieu of kernel drivers, and document the likely outcome for gaming compatibility claims.
rationale: §56.2 notes anti-cheat realities; lockdown makes anti-cheat kernel drivers impossible so gaming claims need an honest position.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Support hardware security keys (FIDO2 hmac-secret) as an additional disk-unlock and login factor.
rationale: Security-conscious enthusiasts targeted at public alpha expect hardware-key unlock and it exercises the pluggable authenticator interface.

lens: Boot, firmware, platform security and identity
text: Question: should system generation switches ever be applied without reboot (kexec into the new kernel or live userspace-only generation switch), given that lockdown forbids unsigned kexec and measured boot values would need re-derivation?
rationale: The answer determines whether the update UX can promise reboot-free updates and constrains the bootloader and PCR policy design.

text: ADR selecting the text shaping and rasterization stack (HarfBuzz+FreeType retained versus Rust-native rustybuzz/swash/cosmic-text) and whether it runs as a shared system text service or an in-component library.
rationale: Every native UI surface, terminal, and compositor overlay depends on this choice and it is nearly impossible to change after the toolkit ships.

text: Font management service that stores fonts as immutable content-addressed package objects, supports per-user installation, exposes a typed FontMatcher interface for family/weight/script fallback chains, and replaces fontconfig for native apps.
rationale: The baseline names text rendering as a requirement but no shipping desktop works without discoverable, installable, fallback-resolved fonts.

text: Select and license a default system font set covering Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari, Thai, CJK, monospace, and color emoji (COLRv1), with a documented coverage matrix.
rationale: A public release that renders tofu for common scripts is not shippable and font licensing must be settled before redistribution.

text: Shared GPU glyph atlas and shaped-text cache delivered as a MemoryObject across components so identical text runs are shaped and rasterized once per system rather than once per component.
rationale: Cheap isolation means many more components render text, so per-component glyph caches would multiply memory and startup cost.

text: Full complex-text support in the toolkit: bidirectional text (UAX #9), line breaking (UAX #14), grapheme segmentation, vertical CJK layout, variable fonts, OpenType features, and emoji sequences, verified against the Unicode conformance test suites.
rationale: International users are a majority of the desktop market and half-working script support is worse than none for trust.

text: Policy decision on hinting, subpixel positioning, and gamma so native and Linux-personality text render identically at every fractional scale factor.
rationale: Mixed-fidelity text between native and compat windows is the most visible signal that a compat app is not native, violating §49.

text: Expose the native font store to the Linux personality through a fontconfig-compatible view and to the Windows personality through the Wine font directory so all three worlds see the same installed fonts.
rationale: Users install a font once and expect every application, native or compat, to see it.

text: Native input-method protocol in the UI toolkit (preedit, commit, surrounding text, cursor rectangle, candidate window placement) where an IME component receives Capability<TextInputFocus> only for the focused field and never a global key stream.
rationale: CJK, Indic, and Vietnamese users cannot type at all without an IME framework, and the capability model forbids the ambient key-logging that existing IMEs rely on.

text: ADR on input-method engines: host existing engines (librime, libpinyin, anthy, libhangul, m17n) inside a sandboxed IME host component versus writing native engines, with the 1.0 language list.
rationale: Writing IMEs from scratch violates §67 principle 15 while shipping without them excludes billions of users.

text: Keyboard layout model that reuses xkeyboard-config data, supports layout switching, compose and dead keys, per-window versus global layout policy, and a layout switcher in the shell.
rationale: Non-US keyboard users need layouts from day one of dogfooding and XKB data is mature and must not be reinvented.

text: Bridge the native IME to Linux apps via zwp_text_input_v3 and an IBus/Fcitx-compatible D-Bus endpoint, and to Windows apps via Wine's IMM32/TSF path, so one active IME types into every window.
rationale: Users switch between native and compat windows constantly and cannot tolerate different IME state per window class.

text: Emoji and special-character picker exposed as a system service invoked by a global shortcut that commits text through the same input-method protocol.
rationale: Every modern desktop ships one and it exercises the IME protocol without a full IME engine.

text: ADR adopting ICU/CLDR (or a Rust ICU4X port) as the locale data source, with Locale as a typed object, per-application locale override, and a tzdata/CLDR package that updates independently of system generations.
rationale: Locale-correct formatting, collation, plural rules and time zones are required for any non-developer user and CLDR/tzdata change more often than the OS.

text: SDK localization pipeline: a message catalog format decision (Fluent versus gettext), catalogs shipped as package resources, build-time extraction tooling, and a public translation platform for first-party apps.
rationale: Translations cannot be bolted on later without rewriting every UI string site, and community translation is how small OS projects reach 1.0 language counts.

text: Right-to-left layout mirroring, locale-aware date/number/currency/collation APIs, and a target set of fully translated 1.0 languages with a published percent-translated gate.
rationale: 1.0 must define which users it actually serves and RTL mirroring is an architectural toolkit property, not a translation.

text: Spell-checking, hyphenation, and dictionary service (Hunspell dictionaries as packages) exposed as a typed interface consumed by the toolkit's text fields.
rationale: Users expect red underlines in every text field and the dictionaries must be installable per language.

text: ADR defining the accessibility tree model (roles, states, properties, actions, live regions, text ranges) shared between the UI toolkit and semantic interfaces, and whether to adopt AccessKit as the schema and bridge.
rationale: The baseline mentions accessibility metadata but not the actual tree contract that screen readers, automation, and testing all consume.

text: Assistive technology access is a capability: an AT component receives Capability<AccessibilityTree> scoped by user consent, with password and secure fields redacted unless the AT holds an elevated grant.
rationale: Existing accessibility buses are an ambient keylogging and screen-scraping vector, which contradicts §9 and would be the largest hole in the security model.

text: Native screen reader component with a text-to-speech service (engine decision: espeak-ng, Piper, or vendor voices) supporting braille output via BRLTTY-equivalent drivers.
rationale: An OS that blind users cannot operate is not a public stable release and the compatibility layers cannot supply a native screen reader.

text: System-wide accessibility settings enforced by the toolkit: screen magnifier, high contrast, large text, reduced motion, color filters, cursor size, sticky/slow/bounce keys, mouse keys, and dwell click.
rationale: These are legal requirements in many markets and are cheap when built into the toolkit but impossible to retrofit into third-party apps.

text: Accessibility bridges so the native screen reader can read Linux apps via AT-SPI2 and Windows apps via UI Automation/MSAA exposed by Wine.
rationale: Most 1.0 apps will be compat apps and they must be accessible or the whole desktop is not.

text: Accessibility conformance gate: shell, installer, greeter, lock screen, and every first-party app pass an EN 301 549 / WCAG 2.2 AA equivalent checklist and the screen reader works from the first installer screen.
rationale: A user who needs a screen reader must be able to install the OS unassisted or accessibility is a marketing claim.

text: ADR on printing architecture: IPP Everywhere / driverless-first native print service with PDF as the spool format, CUPS confined to the Linux personality for legacy drivers, and a print job modelled as a typed Operation.
rationale: Printing is a top support burden on every desktop and the baseline never mentions it.

text: OS-owned print dialog and printer discovery (mDNS/DNS-SD, USB, WSD) that grants Capability<PrintJob> for a single job the same way the file chooser grants file authority.
rationale: Apps must not receive ambient printer enumeration or spooler access, so the dialog must be a system authority like the file chooser.

text: Scanning service supporting driverless eSCL/WSD and SANE backends, exposing Capability<Scanner> via a system scan dialog, with a first-party document scanner app.
rationale: Home and office users expect scan-to-PDF to work and it shares discovery and authority design with printing.

text: ADR choosing the PDF rendering and generation library (pdfium, poppler, or a Rust renderer) shared by print-to-PDF, print preview, the document viewer, and the file browser thumbnails.
rationale: PDF is the interchange format for printing and documents and one shared sandboxed renderer avoids four copies of the same attack surface.

text: Bridge compat printing: expose the native print service as a CUPS-compatible IPP socket for Linux apps and as the Wine print spooler for Windows apps.
rationale: Compat applications must print to the same printers with the same dialog to satisfy §49.

text: Notification service with a typed Notify interface requiring Capability<Notifications>, actions bound to semantic interfaces instead of callbacks, do-not-disturb and focus modes, persistent history, and survival across compositor restart.
rationale: Notifications are a core desktop primitive, an obvious phishing and spam vector, and the natural first consumer of semantic actions.

text: Compat notification bridges: org.freedesktop.Notifications and portal notification D-Bus for Linux apps and Windows toast/balloon APIs via Wine mapped onto the native service with per-app grants.
rationale: Compat apps must appear in the same notification center and be subject to the same do-not-disturb policy.

text: Clipboard policy ADR: no ambient clipboard read, reads permitted only on a user-initiated paste gesture into the focused surface or via an explicit Capability<ClipboardRead> for clipboard managers, with typed content negotiation and lazy transfer over MemoryObject.
rationale: Clipboard sniffing is the most common data-exfiltration path on existing desktops and the baseline lists clipboard capabilities without defining the policy.

text: Clipboard history and sensitive-item marking so password managers and secure fields can mark entries ephemeral and excluded from history and sync.
rationale: Clipboard history is expected by users but leaks credentials unless the source can flag content.

text: Unified drag-and-drop and clipboard content types across native, Wayland/X11 (wl_data_device, XDND) and Windows (OLE) personalities, where a drop grants the target a capability to the dropped object rather than a path.
rationale: Dragging a file from a native file browser into a Windows app and vice versa is the litmus test for compat feeling native.

text: Decision that X11-style primary selection (middle-click paste) is not a native concept and exists only inside the Linux personality.
rationale: An explicit non-goal prevents a historical Unix behaviour from leaking into the native model per §68.

text: Settings storage model: settings are typed, schema-versioned objects whose changes are recorded as system history events and restorable via os restore, with a per-application settings API in the SDK.
rationale: Without this, §31 system history cannot restore configuration and every app invents its own config file format.

text: Settings application composed of per-panel components (displays, network, Bluetooth, sound, power, users, privacy and permissions, accessibility, keyboard and input methods, printers, date/time, region, appearance, default apps, about) each holding only its panel's capabilities.
rationale: Users cannot configure a desktop from the command line and the panel-per-component design dogfoods §11.

text: Default-application, URL-scheme, and content-type association registry exposed as a typed interface so opening a file or link launches the user-chosen handler with a capability to just that object.
rationale: Double-clicking a file or link is the primary way users start apps and it must route through capabilities, not path-based MIME databases.

text: Appearance model: light/dark, accent colour, icon and cursor themes, wallpaper, and font scale exposed to native apps as typed settings and to Linux apps via the settings portal and GTK/Qt platform hints.
rationale: Inconsistent theming between native and compat windows is immediately visible and portals are the accepted channel for it.

text: Desktop shell: panel/taskbar, launcher with search, virtual workspaces, window switcher, overview, quick-settings, status indicators (network, battery, volume, Bluetooth, input method) and a status-tray policy ADR (StatusNotifierItem compat versus none).
rationale: §62 calls for a polished shell without enumerating its parts, and the tray decision affects many Linux and Windows apps.

text: Session management: login greeter, fast user switching, logout/shutdown/reboot flows with inhibitors, session restore that reopens windows from system history, and optional auto-login.
rationale: Multi-user login and a coherent power-off flow are baseline expectations and interact with generations, disk encryption, and identity.

text: Screen lock as a compositor-enforced state: no application surface renders above the lock, authentication via the SEC identity service (password, fingerprint, smartcard), idle-triggered lock, lock-before-suspend, and notification privacy on the lock screen.
rationale: A lock screen that can be bypassed by a crashed locker process is a classic desktop vulnerability that the compositor-owned design avoids.

text: Idle and sleep inhibition modelled as Capability<InhibitIdle> and Capability<InhibitSuspend> granted per app and visible in the shell, replacing ambient inhibitor D-Bus calls.
rationale: Video playback and downloads must keep the screen on, but uncontrolled inhibitors are how battery drains silently on today's desktops.

text: Global shortcut model where apps request named actions bound by the user in Settings and never receive raw global key grabs.
rationale: Push-to-talk, screenshots, and media apps need global keys and the ambient X11 grab model is a keylogger primitive.

text: Basic touchscreen and touchpad gesture support ships, but on-screen keyboard, tablet mode, and convertible form-factor UI are explicitly out of scope for 1.0.
rationale: Constraining scope to desktop and laptop keeps §62's hardware target honest while still handling touchscreens present on target laptops.

text: Time service: NTP/NTS client (decision: chrony retained versus native), RTC synchronisation, timezone auto-detection through a location capability, and defined monotonic versus wall-clock semantics for Operation deadlines across suspend.
rationale: TLS, package signing, and deadlines all fail with wrong clocks and suspend/resume clock behaviour must be defined for the async model.

text: Location service exposing coarse (timezone, Wi-Fi geolocation) and precise location as separate capabilities with a shell indicator while in use.
rationale: Timezone detection, maps, and weather need it and it is one of the most sensitive ambient permissions on existing desktops.

text: Persistent structured system log/journal with retention, per-component attribution, privacy redaction, and export for bug reports, distinct from the low-overhead tracing pipeline.
rationale: §24 covers live tracing but users and crash reporters need durable logs from previous boots.

text: Network management service with connection profiles, ADR on the Wi-Fi supplicant (iwd versus wpa_supplicant versus native Rust), WPA2/WPA3 personal and enterprise EAP, hidden networks, captive-portal detection, and a shell picker.
rationale: V1 daily-driving on laptops requires reliable Wi-Fi and the supplicant choice dictates the security and maintenance surface.

text: Address and name resolution: DHCPv4, IPv6 SLAAC/DHCPv6 with privacy extensions, a system resolver with DNS-over-TLS/HTTPS, DNSSEC validation, mDNS/DNS-SD, and split DNS per interface or VPN.
rationale: A modern desktop that leaks DNS or cannot join an IPv6-only network is not releasable.

text: ADR on the per-application network capability granularity (any, internet-only, local-network, specific hosts/ports, listen) and the default-deny inbound firewall built on retained nftables.
rationale: §9 says no ambient network access but never defines what a network capability is, and the granularity decision shapes every network API.

text: VPN support: WireGuard as the native tunnel primitive, OpenVPN/IPsec/proprietary clients hosted in the Linux personality, tunnels modelled as capabilities with per-app routing policy, and a shell toggle.
rationale: Remote work users cannot adopt an OS without their employer's VPN and always-on VPN interacts with the network capability model.

text: Emulate the NetworkManager D-Bus API and resolv.conf/nsswitch conventions for Linux apps, and propagate proxy settings and connectivity state to Windows apps via Wine's registry and WinINet.
rationale: Browsers, chat clients, and package managers inside the personalities query network state directly and break without these surfaces.

text: Metered-connection flagging, MAC address randomisation, Wi-Fi hotspot and USB/Bluetooth tethering, wired 802.1X, and system proxy configuration.
rationale: These are the laptop networking features enthusiasts check first in a public alpha.

text: ADR on the Bluetooth stack: retain BlueZ as an in-kernel/host pair or move the host stack to a userspace native component per §33, with required profiles A2DP, HFP, HID, LE Audio/LC3, GATT and BLE privacy.
rationale: Bluetooth is the classic userspace-driver candidate and §62 requires it to work on laptops with no design stated.

text: Bluetooth pairing agent and device chooser in the shell that grant apps Capability<BluetoothDevice> per paired device, never adapter-wide scanning authority.
rationale: BLE scanning is a location-tracking vector and pairing UI is unavoidable for headphones, mice and keyboards.

text: ADR on the media framework: sandboxed decoder components fed by a native pipeline versus retaining GStreamer or FFmpeg as the pipeline, with codecs delivered as separately updatable packages.
rationale: Media decoders are the single largest source of memory-safety exploits and are the poster child for §11 component isolation.

text: Hardware video decode and encode (VA-API and Vulkan Video on retained Mesa) exposed through ComputeDevice with decoded frames delivered as MemoryObjects zero-copy to the compositor.
rationale: Software 4K decode drains laptops and the zero-copy chain in §17 is meaningless without a real video path to prove it.

text: Codec shipping and patent policy: which codecs are in the default image (AV1, VP9, Opus, FLAC, Vorbis), which arrive via hardware decoders only (H.264, HEVC), and which are optional user-installed packages.
rationale: Patent exposure decides what a distributed 1.0 image may legally contain and users judge an OS by whether video plays.

text: Protected-content playback strategy: Widevine L3 available through the Linux-personality browser CDM, native CDM integration and L1/secure-path playback declared out of scope for 1.0.
rationale: Netflix and Spotify working in the browser is a user expectation, while L1 requires vendor trust chains the project cannot obtain.

text: Camera service (retain V4L2, ADR on libcamera adoption for laptop ISP pipelines) granting per-session Capability<Camera> with a shell in-use indicator, virtual camera support, and a first-party camera app.
rationale: Video calls are a daily laptop task and camera access is the permission users care about most.

text: Media session interface (play/pause/next, now-playing metadata) surfaced in the shell and bound to hardware media keys and Bluetooth AVRCP, with an MPRIS bridge for Linux apps.
rationale: Media keys and lock-screen controls are expected everywhere and demonstrate a semantic interface used by the shell.

text: OS-owned screenshot and screen-recording tools using the compositor's capture capability, with region selection, annotation, and per-app screen-share picker for compat portals.
rationale: §40 forbids unrestricted capture so the OS itself must supply the tools users would otherwise install.

text: Colour management in the compositor: ICC profile per display, colour-managed surfaces, HDR-to-SDR tone mapping, and a night-light mode.
rationale: HDR support in §40 is incorrect without colour management and creative users will not adopt a desktop that mis-renders colour.

text: ADR on browser strategy for 1.0: ship Chromium and/or Firefox through the Linux personality as the default browser versus investing in a native port, plus a native sandboxed WebView component for apps.
rationale: §56.5 says a browser is existential but the baseline never chooses one, and the choice determines how much Linux-personality polish is on the critical path.

text: Browser integration deliverables: default-browser registration, URL dispatch, downloads into capability-scoped locations, WebRTC camera/microphone through native capabilities, file-chooser portal, and Widevine availability.
rationale: A compat browser that cannot open links from native apps or use the camera is the first thing a public alpha user will report.

text: ADR on the interactive command shell: a POSIX shell inside the Linux personality versus a native object-aware shell that speaks typed interfaces, and how the os CLI, PTYs, and job control map onto tasks and channels.
rationale: Developers live in the terminal from V1 and the shell defines whether the native object model is reachable from the command line.

text: Native terminal emulator: GPU-rendered via the system text stack, tabs and splits, OSC 8 hyperlinks, Sixel/Kitty graphics, true colour, and a PTY bridge so Linux CLI tools run inside a native window.
rationale: §60 lists a terminal but not the feature bar required for developers to abandon their current terminal.

text: Decision on the authority a terminal session confers on Linux programs it launches (an ambient Linux-personality environment scoped by the terminal's own capabilities) and how a developer escalates or attenuates it.
rationale: Terminals are the one place users expect ambient authority and the policy must be explicit or §9 silently erodes.

text: Power and battery UX: battery status and estimates, power profiles (performance, balanced, power-saver) mapped to ResourceDomain energy policy, per-application energy attribution in Settings, low-battery actions, lid-close behaviour, and charge limits.
rationale: §62 requires laptop batteries to work but users judge power management through this UI and per-app attribution is only possible because of resource domains.

text: Thermal and frequency policy daemon (thermald/power-profiles-daemon equivalents) plus laptop function keys, keyboard backlight, and display brightness control exposed as typed settings.
rationale: Without thermal policy the selected laptops throttle or overheat, and hotkeys are the first hardware check reviewers make.

text: UPower and logind D-Bus compatibility (battery state, inhibitors, session and seat queries) for Linux apps, backed by the native power and session services.
rationale: Browsers, media players, and desktop environments inside the Linux personality query these interfaces and misbehave without them.

text: Desktop search and indexing service that indexes only content the user has granted, exposes typed search over files, apps, settings and semantic interfaces, and powers the launcher.
rationale: The launcher search and the AI action graph in §44 both need an index, and an indexer with ambient home-directory access would violate §9.

text: Trash and undo-delete semantics built on storage snapshots, plus removable-media automount, safe eject, and MTP device access granted through the file chooser.
rationale: Users expect a recycle bin and USB sticks to just work, and both are natural applications of the CoW storage model.

text: Network file share providers (SMB, NFS, WebDAV, SFTP) surfaced as storage objects in the file chooser and file browser with credentials in the secrets service.
rationale: Home NAS and office shares are a common adoption blocker and belong in the storage provider model rather than ad hoc mounts.

text: Decide the first-party application set beyond §60 (document/PDF viewer, media player, archive manager, calculator, camera, disk utility, system monitor) and which are native versus bundled compat apps at 1.0.
rationale: Every desktop ships a minimum app set and each native app is a multi-month commitment that must be scheduled against the workstreams.

text: Desktop-essentials latency targets tracked in the benchmark suite: keystroke-to-glyph through the IME path, notification post-to-display, lock-to-unlock, Wi-Fi reconnect after resume, Bluetooth audio connect, and camera cold start.
rationale: §54 tracks kernel and compositor metrics but the metrics users actually feel are these desktop-service latencies.

text: Opt-in usage telemetry policy and implementation (what is collected, anonymisation, retention, user-visible toggle) separate from crash reporting.
rationale: A 1.0 project needs adoption and hardware data but any undisclosed collection would destroy the trust a capability-security OS depends on.

text: Online-account integration (calendar, contacts, mail sync), parental controls, and speech dictation are declared out of scope for 1.0 with only semantic-interface hooks reserved.
rationale: Explicit non-goals stop the desktop-essentials list from expanding indefinitely and let the semantic model host them later.

text: Decide the signing key hierarchy: offline root key, per-channel intermediate release keys, package-publisher keys, and HSM/threshold custody for every key that can sign a system generation.
rationale: Every update, rollback and Secure Boot chain rests on this hierarchy and it cannot be changed after devices have enrolled trust.

text: Reserve signature, signer-identity and trust-policy fields in the package and generation manifest formats before the first immutable install ships.
rationale: Retrofitting signatures into an already-deployed immutable format forces a breaking format migration.

text: Build a trust-store object delivered inside system generations so signing keys can be rotated or revoked without out-of-band user action.
rationale: A leaked release key must be replaceable across the installed base with a normal update.

text: Decide whether released artifacts are recorded in an append-only transparency log (Sigstore/Rekor-style) and whether clients verify inclusion proofs.
rationale: Binary transparency is the only defence against a compromised signing pipeline silently shipping targeted builds.

text: Decide how UEFI Secure Boot is satisfied on retail hardware: Microsoft-signed shim, vendor key enrollment via MOK, or requiring users to enroll project keys.
rationale: Without a decision the OS will not boot on the majority of laptops with factory Secure Boot enabled.

text: Define the kernel module signing policy covering out-of-tree modules, proprietary GPU drivers and locally built modules under Secure Boot.
rationale: NVIDIA users and kernel developers both need a sanctioned path that does not require disabling Secure Boot.

text: Design third-party publisher identity: publisher keys, package-name namespace ownership, key attestation at first publish and key-change handling.
rationale: A public repository without publisher identity cannot prevent name squatting or takeover updates.

text: Decide whether the repository accepts prebuilt binaries from publishers or rebuilds every package from source on project infrastructure.
rationale: This determines whether reproducibility, SBOMs and supply-chain guarantees are project-wide or publisher-dependent.

text: Specify the repository wire protocol and metadata format: content-addressed index, chunk-level fetch, delta hints, and static-file serving so any HTTP host can mirror it.
rationale: The client package manager in V1 cannot be built without a defined server contract.

text: Implement TUF-style metadata roles (root, targets, snapshot, timestamp) so clients detect stale, replayed or mix-and-match repository metadata.
rationale: Signed packages alone do not stop an attacker serving an old vulnerable but validly signed generation.

text: Decide the distribution topology: origin plus commercial CDN, volunteer mirror network with verification, or both, including mirror health checks and geo-selection.
rationale: Public alpha download volume exceeds what a single origin can serve and mirrors must not be able to tamper.

text: Ship chunk-level delta updates between generations using the content-addressed store so an update transfers only new objects.
rationale: Full-image updates of an immutable OS are otherwise multi-gigabyte and unacceptable on laptops and metered links.

text: Decide repository retention: how many past generations and package versions remain downloadable, which bounds the rollback and restore promises.
rationale: System restore to an arbitrary point in history is only honest if the referenced objects still exist somewhere.

text: Build a publisher submission pipeline with manifest validation, requested-capability review, malware and license scanning, and human review queues.
rationale: An app repository is a distribution channel for malware unless submissions are gated.

text: Expose a repository search and metadata API that shows declared capabilities, publisher, SBOM and compatibility status before installation.
rationale: Users can only consent to capability requests if the store surfaces them before install.

text: Support offline installation media and local repository mirrors for air-gapped and lab machines.
rationale: Hardware labs, installer testing and privacy-conscious users need install and update without internet.

text: Define update channels (nightly, testing, stable, LTS) with promotion criteria, minimum soak time and who may promote.
rationale: Internal daily-driving from V1 requires a nightly channel and a defined path for changes to reach stable.

text: Implement staged percentage rollouts with automatic halt when crash-rate or boot-failure telemetry exceeds a threshold.
rationale: A bad kernel or compositor generation must be stopped before it reaches the whole installed base.

text: Implement an emergency pull mechanism that withdraws a published generation from a channel and lets clients step to a newer fixed generation without violating anti-rollback rules.
rationale: Security response needs a fast path to stop distribution of a broken release.

text: Decide client update orchestration: background download, apply-on-reboot versus live activation of userspace generations, metered-network behavior and user deferral.
rationale: Users judge an OS by whether updates interrupt them; this policy shapes the whole updater UX.

text: Define boot-success health criteria and a boot counter so a new generation is only marked good after login, display, network and audio services come up.
rationale: Automatic rollback is meaningless if 'boot succeeded' is decided before the desktop is actually usable.

text: Integrate firmware and microcode updates (LVFS/fwupd-style) into system history so firmware changes are recorded, and rollback limits are explicit.
rationale: Firmware is the one update the generation model cannot roll back and users must be told so.

text: Decide the versioning scheme across the four stability layers (kernel ABI, platform interfaces, SDK, frameworks) and how a system generation number relates to a public release name.
rationale: Bug reports, compatibility claims and LTS policy all need an unambiguous version vocabulary.

text: Decide release cadence and LTS policy: time-based versus feature-based releases, LTS support window, which layers receive backports, and end-of-life notification.
rationale: 1.0 'stable' is a support promise and the promise must be written down before it is made.

text: Define supported upgrade paths between stable releases (N to N+1, skip-version) and test them in CI on real generation histories.
rationale: Users on 1.0 must reach 1.x and 2.0 without reinstalling for the immutable model to be credible.

text: Define the kernel ABI and platform interface deprecation process: announcement, minimum overlap window, tooling to detect use of deprecated interfaces.
rationale: A decades-long ABI still needs a way to retire mistakes without breaking installed software.

text: Decide the upstream Linux tracking cadence: which upstream LTS series to base on, rebase frequency per divergence phase, and automation for stable-branch backports.
rationale: Fork maintenance cost and CVE exposure are determined by this policy from the first commit.

text: Build a CVE ingestion pipeline that pulls kernel CNA and upstream advisories, auto-tags applicability against forked or removed subsystems, and opens triage tasks.
rationale: The kernel CNA issues thousands of CVEs a year and manual triage of a fork will not scale.

text: Publish a security policy with a reporting contact, encrypted channel, disclosure timeline, embargo rules and CNA registration for the project's own CVEs.
rationale: Public alpha invites vulnerability reports and researchers need a defined channel.

text: Publish machine-readable security advisories (OSV and CSAF/VEX) and a feed the updater and third-party scanners can consume.
rationale: Users and downstreams cannot assess exposure from prose advisories.

text: Generate an SBOM (SPDX or CycloneDX) for every package and system generation from the content-addressed dependency graph.
rationale: Vulnerability matching and license compliance both require knowing exactly what is in a generation.

text: Match installed generations against advisories on the client and surface vulnerable packages with the generation that fixes them.
rationale: Security fixes only matter if users learn they are affected and can act.

text: Set security response targets: time from critical CVE disclosure to a stable-channel generation, measured and published per release.
rationale: A stable OS is judged on patch latency and the target must exist to be tracked.

text: Join pre-disclosure coordination lists (linux-distros, GPU and browser vendor programs) and define who holds embargoed information.
rationale: Without pre-disclosure the fork learns of kernel vulnerabilities at the same time as attackers.

text: Build an embargoed build path that can compile, sign and stage a security release privately before public publication.
rationale: Public CI leaks embargoed fixes before coordinated disclosure.

text: Write and rehearse incident runbooks for compromised signing keys, compromised build infrastructure and compromised repository hosts.
rationale: Recovery from a supply-chain compromise must be planned, not improvised while users are exposed.

text: Commission an independent security audit of the capability system, native ABI and update pipeline before 1.0.
rationale: A security model that has only been reviewed by its authors cannot be called stable.

text: Decide whether to run a vulnerability reward program at 1.0 and how it is funded.
rationale: Reward programs materially change report volume and the triage capacity that must be staffed.

text: Define opt-in telemetry policy: exact data schema, consent flow, retention, anonymization, and a public privacy review before anything is collected.
rationale: Staged rollouts and the hardware database depend on telemetry, and collecting it without a policy destroys trust.

text: Build a native crash reporting pipeline that captures component and task-group state, capability graph and trace context as structured reports rather than raw core dumps.
rationale: The OS already knows component semantics and crash reports should use them instead of reconstructing from memory images.

text: Run a symbol server keyed by content hash (debuginfod-compatible) so stripped generations can be symbolicated on demand.
rationale: Debugging a daily-driven V1 build and every later crash report requires symbols for immutable binaries.

text: Capture kernel panics into persistent storage (pstore/kdump) and submit them after the next successful boot.
rationale: Kernel fork regressions are the highest-severity failures and are otherwise invisible to developers.

text: Build crash deduplication, grouping and a triage dashboard that links crash signatures to generations and task IDs.
rationale: Raw crash streams are useless at alpha scale without aggregation.

text: Show users the exact report contents and let them redact before any crash or telemetry submission, and run the telemetry agent with only the capabilities it needs.
rationale: A telemetry agent with ambient authority contradicts the security model it is meant to protect.

text: Collect opt-in compatibility reports for Linux and Windows applications (app identity, personality version, result, workarounds) into a public database.
rationale: Compatibility is a product and users need a ProtonDB-style answer to 'does my software run'.

text: Set a crash-free-session rate and boot-success rate that stable-channel generations must meet as a 1.0 release gate.
rationale: Stability must be a measured number, not a feeling, before the stable label is applied.

text: Define the hardware compatibility database schema: PCI/USB/DMI identifiers, per-generation status, known issues, workarounds and provenance of each entry.
rationale: The baseline names the database but not what it records or how entries are trusted.

text: Ship a hardware probe tool that produces an anonymized device fingerprint and test results that can populate the compatibility database.
rationale: A compatibility database with no ingestion path stays empty.

text: Make the installer query the compatibility database and warn about unsupported or degraded components before writing to disk.
rationale: Alpha users should learn their Wi-Fi card will not work before they wipe their drive.

text: Define hardware support tiers (tested in lab, community reported, unsupported) and the criteria for promoting a device between tiers.
rationale: Constrained target hardware needs a public vocabulary so users know what 'supported' means.

text: Build a physical hardware lab with remote power control, serial and video capture that boots every nightly on each Tier 1 device and runs install, suspend/resume and GPU smoke tests.
rationale: QEMU cannot catch the GPU, firmware and power regressions that break real laptops.

text: Resolve redistribution licensing for firmware blobs, microcode and proprietary drivers, deciding what ships in official images versus a separate non-free repository.
rationale: Shipping Wi-Fi and GPU firmware without redistribution rights blocks any public image.

text: Publish corresponding source for every GPL component of every released generation and automate the source offer from the content-addressed store.
rationale: A Linux kernel fork distributed publicly carries GPL obligations from the first download.

text: Build the install media pipeline: signed, reproducible ISO/USB images per channel with published checksums, nightly builds and automated boot tests of the produced image.
rationale: Developers cannot daily-drive V1 without a repeatable way to produce installable images.

text: Build a download site with verification instructions, signature files and mirror or torrent distribution.
rationale: Public alpha begins with a download and the download must be verifiable.

text: Verify reproducible builds with independent rebuilders and publish per-generation reproducibility status.
rationale: Reproducibility is only a guarantee when someone other than the release pipeline reproduces the bits.

text: Define release-readiness gating: blocker bug definition, exit checklist, go/no-go roles and a freeze policy per channel.
rationale: Without written gates every release decision is renegotiated under time pressure.

text: Generate release notes and hardware-facing changelogs from the task repository and generation diffs rather than hand-written prose.
rationale: Users need to know what changed in a generation, and the task repository already holds the answer.

text: Build a versioned documentation site with API reference generated from the IDL and SDK sources, full-text search and per-release snapshots.
rationale: Developer preview means external developers, and generated references stop docs drifting from interfaces.

text: Decide the documentation taxonomy: user guide, administrator guide, developer guide, ABI specification, architecture and ADR record, compatibility notes, and ownership of each.
rationale: A single undifferentiated docs pile does not serve users, developers and researchers at once.

text: Write migration guides for users coming from Linux distributions and Windows and for developers porting applications to the native SDK.
rationale: Adoption at public alpha depends on explaining what maps to what and what deliberately does not exist.

text: Set up a translation pipeline for OS strings and documentation with contributor tooling and per-release string freeze.
rationale: A public desktop OS shipped in one language excludes most potential users.

text: Decide code hosting (self-hosted forge versus GitHub) and repository layout (monorepo versus per-workstream repositories) including where the Markdown task repository lives.
rationale: Every CI, review and contribution process from V0 onward depends on this choice.

text: Decide contributor licensing terms (DCO versus CLA) and the outbound license for native kernel code alongside inherited GPLv2 code.
rationale: Mixing Rust native code with GPL Linux code has licensing consequences that must be settled before external contributions arrive.

text: Define issue triage: severity and priority labels, hardware and personality tags, templates that capture generation ID and diagnostics, response-time targets and a stale policy.
rationale: Public alpha issue volume will bury the team without a triage process defined earlier.

text: Ship a built-in bug reporter that bundles generation ID, hardware fingerprint, relevant traces and inspect output with user-controlled redaction.
rationale: Good bug reports require data users cannot be expected to gather by hand.

text: Provide an os bisect tool that steps between generations to locate the generation that introduced a regression.
rationale: Immutable generations make regression bisection cheap and it turns vague reports into actionable ones.

text: Stand up community channels (forum, chat, announcement feed, mailing list), a code of conduct and moderation roles before public alpha.
rationale: Public users need somewhere to ask questions that is not the issue tracker.

text: Document and CI-test building the entire OS from source both on a Linux host and on the OS itself, with the contributor path kept to a small fixed number of steps.
rationale: Self-hosting is the V1 goal and onboarding friction decides whether contributors stay.

text: Run a public benchmark dashboard fed by CI with per-commit history and regression alerting for every metric in the performance requirements.
rationale: Performance claims must be continuously measured and publicly visible to be believed.

text: Define all release infrastructure as code with a status page and monitoring, and decide whether the infrastructure itself must run on the OS.
rationale: Repository or CDN outages block updates and security fixes for the entire installed base.

text: Publish a trademark and branding policy for derivatives, remixes and unofficial builds.
rationale: Immutable generations make remixing easy and users must be able to tell official builds from forks.

text: Assess export control and cryptography distribution obligations for the download site and mirrors.
rationale: An OS with disk encryption distributed worldwide has legal obligations that cannot be ignored at public alpha.

text: Estimate and plan funding for ongoing infrastructure cost (CDN bandwidth, build farm, hardware lab, signing hardware) through 1.0 and beyond.
rationale: Release infrastructure has recurring cost and a stable release implies it stays online.

text: Do not build enterprise fleet management, MDM or centralized policy provisioning for 1.0.
rationale: 1.0 targets individual desktops and laptops; fleet tooling would divert effort from the core update and security pipeline.

text: Do not operate a project-owned global mirror network for 1.0; rely on CDN plus verified volunteer mirrors.
rationale: Content addressing and signed metadata make untrusted mirrors safe, so owning mirrors buys little.

text: Run organized pre-release testing rounds with published test cases for installer, updater, rollback and compatibility personalities before each stable release.
rationale: Structured community testing catches hardware and workflow issues the lab matrix cannot cover.

text: The installer must detect existing Windows, Linux and (Intel Mac) macOS installations and offer a non-destructive shrink-and-install-alongside flow that preserves every foreign partition and boot entry.
rationale: Almost every enthusiast who tries a new OS in its first year does so alongside an existing OS; a wipe-only installer caps adoption at zero-risk-tolerance users.

text: Decide the EFI System Partition policy: reuse the existing ESP (including undersized 100 MB OEM ESPs) versus creating a dedicated ESP, and how generation boot entries are laid out in each case.
rationale: Generation-per-boot-entry needs ESP space that Windows-created ESPs often lack, and a wrong choice breaks dual-boot on shipped laptops.

text: The bootloader must chain-load Windows Boot Manager and foreign Linux bootloaders, and self-heal when a Windows update rewrites the UEFI BootOrder or overwrites the fallback bootx64.efi.
rationale: Windows routinely reclaims the default boot entry; without recovery logic dual-boot users lose access to JakeOS after the first Windows patch.

text: Expose JakeOS installations to foreign bootloaders through Boot Loader Specification entries and an os-release-compatible descriptor so os-prober and systemd-boot on a co-installed Linux distro can list JakeOS generations.
rationale: Coexistence is bidirectional: a user whose distro's GRUB cannot see JakeOS will assume the install failed.

text: Decide the Secure Boot strategy for dual-boot machines: Microsoft-signed shim with MOK enrolment, user-enrolled platform keys, or both, with the constraint that Windows Secure Boot and BitLocker remain functional.
rationale: Requiring users to disable Secure Boot silently breaks Windows BitLocker and Windows 11 attestation on the same disk.

text: The installer must detect BitLocker-protected volumes and TPM-sealed Windows disks, explain that boot-chain changes may trigger BitLocker recovery, and require the user to record the recovery key before proceeding.
rationale: BitLocker recovery lockout after installing a second OS is the single most common data-loss report for dual-boot installs.

text: Decide the hardware clock policy (UTC versus local time) and time-sync behaviour for machines shared with Windows so clocks do not drift by the timezone offset on every reboot.
rationale: The RTC localtime mismatch is a decades-old dual-boot annoyance that a new OS can fix by default rather than inherit.

text: Detect NTFS volumes left dirty or hibernated by Windows Fast Startup, refuse read-write mounting of them, and guide the user to disable Fast Startup when a shared data partition is desired.
rationale: Writing to a hibernated NTFS volume corrupts the Windows filesystem, and the OS must protect users from it rather than document it.

text: Ship a live-boot USB image that runs a full desktop session from removable media without touching internal disks and produces a hardware compatibility report before the user commits to installing.
rationale: Try-before-install is how users evaluate whether their GPU, Wi-Fi and touchpad work, and is the primary source of hardware database submissions.

text: Provide installation-media creation tooling for Windows, macOS and Linux hosts (or vetted third-party tool instructions) with mandatory image checksum and signature verification.
rationale: The first step of adoption happens on someone else's OS; a broken or unverifiable USB-writing step loses users before boot.

text: Support unattended installation from a declarative answer file covering disk layout, user, locale, network and generation channel.
rationale: The CI hardware test matrix, labs and fleet deployments cannot depend on a human clicking through the installer.

text: Provide a supported uninstall path that removes JakeOS boot entries, restores the previous default bootloader, reclaims partitions and exports user data in standard formats.
rationale: Users adopt an OS more readily when leaving is demonstrably safe; lock-in by omission damages trust in an alpha.

text: Set and measure an installation target: full install to first login in under 10 minutes on reference hardware from USB 3 media, tracked in the benchmark suite.
rationale: Installation time is the first performance impression a user forms and is trivially comparable to Windows and mainstream distros.

text: Decide the on-disk partition and volume layout for generations, content-addressed store, user data, swap/hibernate and recovery, including registered GPT partition type GUIDs.
rationale: Layout must be fixed before V0.5 generations exist, and foreign tools (GParted, Windows Disk Management) must be able to identify JakeOS partitions unambiguously.

text: Decide whether an existing Linux /home partition can be adopted in place by the Linux personality versus copied into the native storage model, and what the user sees in each case.
rationale: Large existing home directories make copy-only migration impractical and adoption by Linux users depends on the answer.

text: Build a migration assistant that imports user data from an on-disk or attached Windows profile (Documents, Pictures, Desktop, Downloads, Music, Videos, browser profiles) into native collections with progress, resumability and post-copy verification.
rationale: Windows-to-JakeOS is the largest addressable migration and users will not switch without their files following them.

text: Build Linux-home import covering XDG user directories, dotfiles, SSH and GPG keys, git configuration and shell history, with per-item choice of destination (Linux personality home versus native application data).
rationale: The earliest adopters are Linux developers whose entire workflow lives in a home directory.

text: Decide how legacy user data maps between the three views: native capability-scoped Collections, the Linux personality POSIX home, and the Windows personality C:\Users profile, so one Documents folder is one set of objects.
rationale: Without a single mapping users end up with three diverging copies of their files and no idea which app sees which.

text: Support macOS migration by importing from Time Machine backups on external drives and from a macOS host over the local network; decide whether read-only APFS access is in scope for 1.0.
rationale: Intel Mac owners facing end of macOS support are a natural audience, and their data is only reachable via Time Machine or APFS.

text: Import browser bookmarks, history, saved passwords and extensions from Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari profiles into whatever browser the browser strategy selects.
rationale: The browser is where most users' daily state lives; losing passwords is a switch-back trigger.

text: Determine whether Wi-Fi credentials can be imported from NetworkManager keyfiles and Windows WLAN profiles (DPAPI-encrypted) during migration, or whether the user must re-enter them.
rationale: Being offline immediately after migration blocks every subsequent onboarding step.

text: Share Bluetooth pairing keys between JakeOS and a co-installed Windows or Linux so peripherals stay paired across dual boot.
rationale: Re-pairing a mouse and headphones on every OS switch is a well-known reason dual-boot users abandon the secondary OS.

text: Detect existing Steam libraries, Wine prefixes, Proton compatdata and Bottles/Lutris configurations on attached volumes and adopt them in the Windows personality without re-download.
rationale: Gaming is a stated major objective and a 500 GB re-download is a decisive adoption barrier.

text: Every migration import is recorded as a system history event with a pre-import snapshot so it can be undone with the standard restore operation.
rationale: Migration is the riskiest operation a new user performs and must be as reversible as an OS update.

text: Provide converters from docker-compose.yml and devcontainer.json to environment.yaml, reporting unsupported constructs explicitly.
rationale: Developers will not hand-rewrite dozens of project environments to try os env.

text: Decide which Linux packaging formats the Linux personality supports for end-user installation (Flatpak, AppImage, deb/rpm via distro container, Nix) and which is the recommended first-class path.
rationale: Linux compatibility is a product, and users need a predictable answer to how to install their existing software.

text: Support machine-to-machine migration: restore a system history point (generations, packages, configuration, user data) onto different hardware from a backup target.
rationale: Hardware replacement is the moment most users are forced to re-evaluate their OS choice, and restoring in place is a differentiator.

text: Retain the in-kernel NTFS read/write driver with a policy for dirty volumes, missing chkdsk, and Windows permission/ACL mapping into the native storage layer.
rationale: Dual-boot users and external drives from Windows machines are NTFS-formatted; read-only support is insufficient for a shared data partition.

text: Support exFAT and FAT32 for removable media including formatting, safe eject, and the timestamp/character-set limitations of each.
rationale: Cameras, SD cards, USB sticks and console storage are exFAT by industry agreement.

text: Decide how the capability-based storage model degrades on foreign filesystems lacking its metadata: xattr fallback, case-insensitivity, forbidden characters, timestamp precision and permission bits.
rationale: Native Collections on NTFS or exFAT must behave predictably or users lose metadata silently when copying across volumes.

text: Removable and foreign volumes are surfaced as user-consented, capability-scoped collections rather than ambient mounts, and appear under conventional /media and drive-letter paths only inside personalities.
rationale: Plugging in a USB stick is where ambient authority typically re-enters a capability system; the policy must exist before V2 hardware work.

text: Decide the recommended format for a dual-boot shared data partition (exFAT versus NTFS) and have the installer offer to create one.
rationale: Dual-boot users need one place both OSes can write, and the recommendation determines which filesystem drivers must be hardened.

text: Unlock and mount LUKS, ext4, Btrfs and XFS volumes from other Linux installations, and decide whether BitLocker volumes are readable via dislocker-style user-space support.
rationale: Reading the previous OS's encrypted disk is a prerequisite for in-place migration.

text: Provide case-insensitive, case-preserving filesystem semantics for the Windows personality's view of user data without imposing them on native or Linux views.
rationale: Win32 applications break on case-sensitive storage and gaming compatibility depends on it.

text: Provide an SMB/CIFS client (SMB2/3, NTLM and Kerberos, DFS) exposing shares as capability-scoped network collections and as UNC paths and mounts inside personalities.
rationale: Home NAS boxes, Windows shares and office networks are SMB; a desktop that cannot browse them is not a desktop.

text: Decide whether 1.0 ships an SMB server for sharing folders to Windows and macOS clients, and if so whether it is Samba in the Linux personality or a native service.
rationale: Sharing files to other machines on a LAN is expected desktop behaviour, but a Samba dependency shapes the personality boundary.

text: Provide mDNS/DNS-SD discovery and .local resolution as a native service, with Avahi and Bonjour API compatibility for Linux and Windows personality applications.
rationale: Printers, NAS, cast targets and developer tooling all depend on zero-configuration discovery.

text: Provide an NFS client and WebDAV client for network filesystems.
rationale: Linux-heavy home labs and Nextcloud users rely on these and expect them from any Linux-derived system.

text: Define a native storage-provider interface so cloud storage (OneDrive, Google Drive, Dropbox, Nextcloud) appears as capability-scoped collections with on-demand hydration, and decide which providers ship in 1.0.
rationale: Migrating users' files increasingly live in cloud sync services rather than on disk.

text: Support IPP Everywhere/AirPrint network printers, SMB-shared Windows printers and driverless scanning (eSCL) discovered via mDNS.
rationale: Printing is the classic adoption-killer for alternative desktops and mixed-OS households share printers.

text: Support MTP/PTP and local phone-to-desktop transfer for Android and iOS devices.
rationale: Photo import from phones is a top-five desktop task and the first thing a switched user tries.

text: Decide whether RDP and VNC clients and a remote-desktop server built on remote surfaces are in scope for 1.0.
rationale: Remote access to Windows machines and headless boxes is how many technical users bridge a partial migration.

text: Active Directory domain join, Group Policy and enterprise fleet management are explicitly out of scope for 1.0.
rationale: Stating the nongoal stops enterprise-shaped requirements from distorting the identity and settings model before the desktop is stable.

text: Support fwupd/LVFS-compatible firmware updates for UEFI, SSDs, docks and peripherals.
rationale: Users must not need to boot Windows to update firmware, and reference laptops ship firmware fixes through LVFS.

text: Decide the fallback virtualization product: a KVM-based VM manager with native UI for running Windows, Linux and other guests when software cannot run under a personality, and its 1.0 feature scope.
rationale: Personalities will never cover 100% of software, and an explicit VM fallback is what lets a user commit to JakeOS as their only OS.

text: Each VM is a Component within a ResourceDomain whose host access (folders, devices, network, clipboard) is granted through capabilities and visible in os inspect.
rationale: Virtualization is the largest ambient-authority hole in every existing desktop and must not become one here.

text: Decide the depth of guest-window integration: individual guest application windows as native surfaces with clipboard, drag/drop, file chooser and notification bridging, versus a single VM display.
rationale: Compatibility must feel native per §49, and seamless mode determines the guest-agent protocol that must be designed early.

text: Evaluate GPU acceleration paths for guests (virtio-gpu Venus/virgl, SR-IOV, full passthrough with multi-GPU) and their viability for a VM gaming fallback.
rationale: The main reason users keep a Windows partition is GPU-bound software the personality cannot run.

text: Evaluate booting an existing physical Windows dual-boot partition as a VM guest, including activation, TPM and BitLocker implications.
rationale: Reusing the Windows partition both ways removes the reboot cost from dual-boot and is a strong migration bridge.

text: Ship guest tools (shared folders, clipboard, time sync, display resize, guest agent) for Windows and Linux guests, and never redistribute Windows images or license keys.
rationale: A fallback VM is unusable without guest integration, and the licensing boundary must be explicit for a public release.

text: Make JakeOS run well as a guest under QEMU/KVM, VirtualBox, VMware, Hyper-V and UTM with virtio drivers, guest agents and dynamic resolution, and publish ready-made VM images.
rationale: Most developers and reviewers will first try the OS inside a VM on their current machine; V1 self-hosting also depends on it.

text: Build a compatibility triage flow: when an ELF or PE binary fails under a personality the OS explains why, consults a public per-application compatibility database, and offers the VM fallback or known workarounds.
rationale: Silent failure of a double-clicked .exe contradicts §49 and leaves users with no next step.

text: Maintain a public, versioned compatibility corpus of the top Linux and Windows applications and games with pass/fail status per generation, fed by CI and opt-in user reports.
rationale: Compatibility claims without a tracked corpus are unverifiable and regressions go unnoticed.

text: Publicly document games and applications blocked by kernel-level anti-cheat, and treat anti-cheat bypass as an explicit nongoal.
rationale: Gamers evaluating the OS need an honest answer up front, and the project must not pursue evasion.

text: Provide a cross-compilation SDK and emulator/VM harness so native applications can be built and tested from Linux, macOS and Windows hosts and in hosted CI without running JakeOS.
rationale: Developers will not adopt a platform they must install to compile for; the first native apps will be built from other OSes.

text: Set an onboarding target: a new developer goes from SDK download to a running hello-component in under 15 minutes on any major host OS, measured by timed onboarding sessions each release.
rationale: Time-to-first-component is the strongest predictor of whether a developer continues.

text: Publish a porting guide mapping POSIX and Win32 concepts to native primitives (file descriptors to capabilities, fork to Components, signals to cancellation, sockets to channels) with worked ports of real applications.
rationale: Every developer arriving has a Unix or Windows mental model and the native model is only adoptable if the translation is written down.

text: Decide whether and how a Linux-personality application may incrementally adopt native interfaces (file chooser, semantic interfaces, capabilities) as an explicit bridge, and what limits keep this from eroding the §3 firewall.
rationale: An all-or-nothing rewrite requirement means no existing application ever becomes native.

text: Provide LSP-based tooling, a Debug Adapter Protocol debugger for components, and remote-development integration (VS Code, JetBrains) into a JakeOS VM or device.
rationale: Developers keep their editors; the OS must meet them there rather than require a new IDE.

text: Provide a one-command reproducible build of the kernel fork and system image from a mainstream Linux host, documented as the contributor entry point.
rationale: OS contributors must be productive before the OS can self-host, and the build path is the first thing they hit.

text: Publish a five-minute guide and tooling for running an existing Linux application on JakeOS via the personality, as the recommended first developer experience.
rationale: Showing existing software working is the fastest credibility win before anyone writes native code.

text: Define the package submission workflow: developer identity and signing key enrolment, automated review (capability manifest linting, malware and license scanning, reproducibility check), human review policy and appeal path.
rationale: A public alpha repository without a submission process accumulates unreviewed packages and becomes a malware vector.

text: Decide the repository model: curated store, open repository, third-party repositories and sideloading, and how trust level is displayed to users for each source.
rationale: This shapes package identity, signing and the permissions UI and cannot be retrofitted after third parties publish.

text: Decide the package naming and identity scheme (reverse-DNS or similar), verified publisher identity, and trademark and name-squatting policy.
rationale: Impersonation of popular applications is the first abuse a public repository faces.

text: Decide the policy for repackaging third-party Linux and Windows software (Flatpak, Wine wrappers, installers) into repository packages, including redistribution licensing and who owns the wrapper.
rationale: Compatibility packages will dominate the early catalogue and their legal and quality status must be settled.

text: Publish AppStream-compatible catalogue metadata and a mirrorable repository protocol so Linux personality software centres and offline installation media can consume the repository.
rationale: Interoperating with existing metadata standards avoids re-authoring every application description.

text: Provide an os publish CLI and hosted CI integrations (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI) that build, sign and submit packages.
rationale: Developers publish from CI, not from a desktop; friction here directly limits catalogue growth.

text: Provide package revocation and emergency withdrawal that propagates through update channels and marks affected generations, with a coordinated disclosure process for third-party application vulnerabilities.
rationale: A public repository must be able to pull a malicious or vulnerable package faster than users install it.

text: Paid applications, in-app purchases and developer payouts are out of scope for 1.0.
rationale: Payments bring legal, tax and fraud obligations that would consume release engineering before the free catalogue is healthy.

text: Publish a tiered known-good hardware list (reference, supported, community-reported) with component-level guidance on GPUs, Wi-Fi chipsets, fingerprint readers and docks, regenerated from the hardware compatibility database each release.
rationale: Users buying a machine for JakeOS need a purchase answer, and the constrained target hardware policy in §62 must be communicated.

text: Decide vendor priorities for purchase guidance (AMD graphics first, Intel and MediaTek Wi-Fi, NVIDIA and Broadcom as best-effort) and state them publicly.
rationale: Honest vendor guidance prevents a wave of unsupported-hardware bug reports at public alpha.

text: Ship a pre-purchase and pre-install compatibility checker that inventories PCI, USB, ACPI and firmware identifiers from the live image or from a Windows/Linux host and reports against the compatibility database.
rationale: Users must know before wiping a disk whether their machine works, and the checker doubles as the database's data source.

text: Hardware and compatibility report submissions are opt-in, pseudonymous, reviewable by the user before upload, and contain no serial numbers or network identifiers.
rationale: The compatibility database depends on user telemetry, which is only acceptable to the target audience if it is transparent.

text: Decide whether to pursue OEM partnerships or a hardware certification programme before 1.0 or leave it to post-1.0.
rationale: A certified machine is the strongest adoption vector but commits scarce engineering to vendor relations.

text: Decide the policy for shipping patent-encumbered codecs (H.264, HEVC, AAC) and proprietary fonts or font metric substitutes needed for migrated media and documents.
rationale: Migrated photo, video and document libraries are useless if the OS cannot decode or render them, and the legal answer differs by jurisdiction.

text: The installer and migration assistant must be fully screen-reader accessible and localized in the same languages as the desktop.
rationale: Accessibility and localization failures at the first screen exclude users before they reach the accessible desktop.

text: Detect and inherit keyboard layout, locale, timezone and hostname from the existing OS installation during install and migration.
rationale: Re-asking what the machine already knows is the first sign of an OS that does not respect the user's setup.

text: Benchmark interoperability paths against Linux and Windows on the same hardware: NTFS and exFAT throughput, SMB client throughput, VM guest application launch time and GPU fraction, and migration import time per 100 GB with verification.
rationale: §54 requires benchmarks for architectural claims and the compatibility layers are where users most expect regressions.

text: Publish a user-facing support matrix and decision tree describing where a given application runs (native, Linux personality, Windows personality, fallback VM, not at all) and the expected experience in each.
rationale: Users decide to switch based on whether their specific software works, and a single honest page answers that.

text: Legacy BIOS/CSM boot is out of scope; the platform is UEFI-only on x86-64.
rationale: Dropping BIOS removes an entire installer and bootloader matrix and the reference hardware is all UEFI.

text: Decide the policy for third-party user-space drivers and firmware delivered as signed packages, including review, revocation and how they appear in the compatibility database.
rationale: Vendors and community porters must have a channel to add hardware support without forking the OS.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Run a measured IPC fast-path spike comparing shared ring buffers, register-carried small messages, seL4/LRPC-style direct scheduler handoff, and io_uring-style batched submission on identical hardware, and record results in an ADR before Channel<T> kernel semantics are fixed.
rationale: The baseline lists candidate techniques but the 1.0 ABI cannot freeze the channel primitive until one technique is chosen on measured numbers rather than intuition.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Measure same-core versus cross-core channel round-trip separately and decide whether the kernel offers synchronous 'call' semantics (time-slice donation to the callee) in addition to asynchronous send.
rationale: Call semantics change scheduler and ABI shape irreversibly, and cross-core cost often dominates real desktop IPC workloads.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Set a numeric IPC round-trip target (e.g. same-core small-message round-trip under 1 µs, cross-core under 5 µs) as a V0 exit criterion.
rationale: The baseline names component creation and startup targets but leaves IPC, its highest-priority performance subsystem, without a number to hold the design to.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide the userspace capability representation (dense per-component handle-table index vs sparse unforgeable 64-bit token vs sealed-pointer layout reservable for CHERI) through an ADR backed by a prototype of each.
rationale: Handle representation is the most permanent ABI decision and determines whether hardware-assisted enforcement can ever be adopted without breaking binaries.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Prototype and benchmark capability revocation strategies (seL4-style derivation tree walk, indirection/epoch invalidation, lazy check-on-use) at 10^6 derived capabilities and choose one.
rationale: Revocation cost bounds how freely the OS can hand out attenuated capabilities, which is the entire security model.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide the service discovery model (capability namespace object, broker component, or manifest-declared static wiring) by which a component obtains its initial and later capabilities.
rationale: Without a discovery decision every service invents its own bootstrap protocol and ambient authority creeps back in.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Research and decide how capabilities persist across component restart and reboot (sturdy references, revocable persistent grant store, or re-prompt), including which object types may ever be persisted.
rationale: A photo editor that loses access to every previously chosen file on relaunch is unusable, yet persistence weakens revocation guarantees.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Validate the frozen capability ABI on a CHERI emulator (QEMU-CHERI or Morello) as an explicit gate demonstrating that application-visible capability semantics survive hardware enforcement.
rationale: The baseline promises hardware-assist readiness; a concrete test prevents that promise from being an unverified assertion at 1.0.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Produce a machine-checked formal model (e.g. TLA+ or Alloy) of capability derivation, attenuation, transfer and revocation before the ABI freeze.
rationale: Security invariants that must hold for decades should be checked once formally rather than rediscovered through CVEs.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Benchmark component implementation strategies (thin wrapper over task_struct+mm_struct+namespaces, prewarmed address-space templates, dedicated native kernel object) against the tens-to-hundreds-of-microseconds creation target and decide the Phase A implementation.
rationale: The cheap-isolation promise is the project's central bet and must be validated with numbers before applications are architected as component graphs.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide whether every component requires its own hardware address space or whether an intra-address-space component class (Wasm or SFI-based) exists for very fine-grained isolation.
rationale: This determines the lower bound of isolation cost and whether plugins and decoders can be isolated at all on legacy hardware.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Set a per-component memory overhead target (e.g. under 512 KB resident for an idle minimal component) and measure it in V0.
rationale: Component graphs with hundreds of components are only viable if fixed per-component memory cost is bounded.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Prototype task multiplexing models (kernel-notified user scheduling à la UMCG/scheduler activations, pure userspace runtime with async syscalls only, kernel-managed lightweight tasks) with 500,000 live tasks and choose one.
rationale: The Task abstraction and its blocking behaviour cannot enter the ABI until it is known which model meets the scale target.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide how a task that unexpectedly blocks in the kernel (page fault, legacy driver path) is prevented from stalling its worker context, and measure the cost of the chosen mechanism.
rationale: Hidden blocking is the classic failure of user-level threading and would silently break the async-first guarantee.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide the completion delivery mechanism (per-component shared completion ring, per-task wait object, or hybrid) and whether io_uring internals are reused or replaced, with wake-up latency measured for each.
rationale: Operation completion is the hinge between kernel scheduling and the runtime and cannot change after SDK code depends on it.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Define the cancellation state machine for in-flight operations that cannot be aborted (DMA already issued, GPU work submitted) and prototype it against a real NVMe read.
rationale: Uniform cancellation is promised, but hardware makes some operations uncancellable and the contract must say what the caller observes.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide the deadline and timestamp representation in the ABI (clock domain, resolution, overflow horizon) including how deadlines survive suspend/resume.
rationale: Every operation carries a deadline, so this small decision is stamped into the permanent ABI.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Prototype MemoryObject ownership transfer over candidate backings (shmem/memfd, dma-buf, dedicated native object) and measure transfer cost for 4 KB and 64 MB objects including TLB shootdown.
rationale: Zero-copy dataflow is only real if transfer is cheaper than copying at realistic sizes.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide whether ownership transfer is enforced (kernel unmaps the sender) or advisory (sender promises not to touch), with the measured enforcement cost attached.
rationale: Enforced transfer gives security guarantees but may cost more than a copy for small objects; the semantics must be fixed before SDK types are designed.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
text: Decide whether dma-buf becomes the underlying implementation for DMA- and GPU-compatible MemoryObjects and demonstrate a NIC-to-GPU zero-copy path on target hardware.
rationale: Reusing dma-buf keeps mature GPU drivers working; the end-to-end demo proves the §17 dataflow is achievable rather than aspirational.

lens: Research spikes and decisions that must precede commitments
